chem_edx.3.12.summary: In electrolysis, **oxidation is the loss of electrons** and **reduction is the gain of electrons** (OIL RIG). Positive ions (cations) move to the negative cathode and gain electrons, so **reduction always happens at the cathode**; negative ions (anions) move to the positive anode and lose electrons, so **oxidation always happens at the anode**. Because one electrode gives electrons to the circuit and the other takes them away, electrolysis is a redox process: oxidation and reduction always happen together.

core.h: Oxidation and reduction in terms of electrons
core.p: Earlier you met oxidation as gaining oxygen and reduction as losing oxygen. In electrolysis we need a more powerful definition based on **electrons**, because many electrode reactions do not involve oxygen at all (for example bromide ions turning into bromine).
bullets: **Oxidation is the loss of electrons.**
**Reduction is the gain of electrons.**
A species that loses electrons is **oxidised**; a species that gains electrons is **reduced**.
Electrons are negative, so losing them makes a particle's charge **more positive**; gaining them makes it **more negative** (or less positive).
Example of oxidation: 2Br- → Br2 + 2e- (each bromide ion loses one electron).
Example of reduction: Pb2+ + 2e- → Pb (each lead ion gains two electrons).

callouts.p: Oxidation is the loss of electrons.
Reduction is the gain of electrons.

core.p: The quickest way to remember the definitions is **OIL RIG**: **O**xidation **I**s **L**oss, **R**eduction **I**s **G**ain (of electrons). Always say 'of electrons' in an answer, because 'loss' on its own could mean loss of oxygen, which is the opposite idea.
bullets: OIL = Oxidation Is Loss of electrons.
RIG = Reduction Is Gain of electrons.
Electrons appear on the **right-hand side** of an oxidation half equation (they are a product, given away).
Electrons appear on the **left-hand side** of a reduction half equation (they are a reactant, taken in).
This is a quick check in the exam: find where the e- is written, and you know which process it is.

callouts.p: e- on the left = gained = reduction. e- on the right = lost = oxidation.

core.p: In electrolysis the **anode** is the **positive electrode** and the **cathode** is the **negative electrode**. Opposite charges attract, so ions move towards the electrode of opposite charge.
bullets: **Cations** (positive ions, e.g. metal ions and H+) are attracted to the **cathode** (negative).
**Anions** (negative ions, e.g. Cl-, Br-, OH-) are attracted to the **anode** (positive).
Memory aid: **PANIC** = Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.
Second memory aid: **AN OX and a RED CAT** = ANode OXidation, REDuction CAThode.
The electrode names stay the same whatever the electrolyte is.

callouts.p: Reduction occurs at the cathode and oxidation occurs at the anode in electrolysis.

core.h: Why reduction happens at the cathode
core.p: The cathode is connected to the **negative terminal** of the d.c. power supply, so the power supply pushes a **surplus of electrons** onto it. When a positive ion touches the cathode it **picks up electrons** from it and becomes a neutral atom or molecule.
bullets: Electrons are supplied to the cathode by the external circuit.
Cations arrive and **gain electrons**, so they are **reduced**.
Metal ions are reduced to metal atoms: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu; Na+ + e- → Na (in molten NaCl).
Hydrogen ions are reduced to hydrogen gas: 2H+ + 2e- → H2.
The number of electrons gained equals the charge on the ion (2+ needs 2e-).

core.h: Why oxidation happens at the anode
core.p: The anode is connected to the **positive terminal**, which **pulls electrons away** from it. When a negative ion reaches the anode it **gives up its extra electrons** to the electrode, and these electrons flow away round the circuit.
bullets: Anions arrive and **lose electrons**, so they are **oxidised**.
Halide ions are oxidised to halogen molecules: 2Cl- → Cl2 + 2e-; 2Br- → Br2 + 2e-.
Hydroxide ions are oxidised to oxygen: 4OH- → O2 + 2H2O + 4e-.
Two halide ions are needed because halogens are **diatomic** (Cl2, Br2).
The electrons released travel through the wire back to the power supply.

callouts.p: The anode is positive, but that does not mean positive ions go there. Positive ions go to the negative cathode.

core.p: A reaction where **oxidation and reduction happen at the same time** is called a **redox** reaction. In electrolysis the electrons lost at the anode are the same electrons, pushed round by the power supply, that are gained at the cathode. So the total number of electrons lost always equals the total number gained.
bullets: Redox = **red**uction + **ox**idation together.
Electrons flow through the **external wire** from the anode to the cathode (via the power supply).
Inside the electrolyte, charge is carried by **moving ions**, not electrons.
Overall equation = oxidation half equation + reduction half equation, with electrons cancelled.
Example (molten PbBr2): Pb2+ + 2Br- → Pb + Br2.

callouts.p: Electrons lost at the anode = electrons gained at the cathode. This is why the amounts of products are linked.

core.p: Molten lead(II) bromide, PbBr2, is the classic binary compound used to show oxidation and reduction. When melted the ions are free to move: Pb2+ and Br-.
bullets: At the cathode (-): Pb2+ + 2e- → Pb. Lead ions **gain** electrons, so are **reduced**. Silvery molten lead collects.
At the anode (+): 2Br- → Br2 + 2e-. Bromide ions **lose** electrons, so are **oxidised**. Red-brown bromine vapour forms.
Lead ions are reduced; bromide ions are oxidised.
Overall: PbBr2 → Pb + Br2.

core.h: Aqueous solutions: same rule, different products
core.p: In a solution there are also H+ and OH- ions from water, so the products may change. But the rule does not change: **whatever forms at the cathode was made by reduction, whatever forms at the anode was made by oxidation**.
bullets: Sodium chloride solution, cathode: 2H+ + 2e- → H2 (reduction).
Sodium chloride solution, anode: 2Cl- → Cl2 + 2e- (oxidation).
Copper sulfate solution (inert electrodes), cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu (reduction).
Copper sulfate solution (inert electrodes), anode: 4OH- → O2 + 2H2O + 4e- (oxidation).
Sodium sulfate or dilute sulfuric acid: H2 at cathode (reduction), O2 at anode (oxidation).

core.p: A **half equation** shows what happens to one species at one electrode, including the electrons. To label it as oxidation or reduction, look at which side the electrons are on and at the change in charge.
bullets: Step 1: write the ion and the product (e.g. Cl- and Cl2).
Step 2: balance the atoms (2Cl- → Cl2).
Step 3: balance the charge with electrons: left is 2-, right is 0, so add 2e- to the right.
Step 4: electrons on the right = **lost** = **oxidation**.
Check: the total charge on both sides must be equal (2- = 0 + 2(-1)).
For oxygen: 4OH- → O2 + 2H2O + 4e- (charge 4- on both sides).

callouts.p: Half equations are mainly Higher tier, but every student must be able to say which electrode has oxidation and which has reduction.

core.h: Oxidation and reduction in terms of charge change
core.p: You can also spot the process from how the charge changes. Losing a negative electron makes something more positive, so the charge goes **up**. Gaining an electron makes the charge go **down**.
bullets: Br- (charge -1) → Br (0): charge rises, so oxidation.
Cu2+ (charge +2) → Cu (0): charge falls, so reduction.
Na → Na+ would be oxidation (charge rises) - this happens when sodium reacts, not at a cathode.
At a cathode the charge on a cation always falls to zero; at an anode the charge on an anion always rises to zero.
This links to Topic 4: in displacement reactions the more reactive metal is oxidised.

core.h: Linking to the older oxygen definition
core.p: The electron definition is more general but agrees with the oxygen one. When metals react with oxygen, the metal atoms lose electrons to form positive ions, so gaining oxygen and losing electrons go together.
bullets: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO: magnesium gains oxygen and also loses electrons (Mg → Mg2+ + 2e-), so it is oxidised both ways.
Oxygen gains electrons (O2 + 4e- → 2O2-), so it is reduced.
In electrolysis, oxygen made at the anode comes from OH- **losing** electrons - oxidation - even though nothing has gained oxygen.
In exams about electrolysis, always use the **electron** definition.

callouts.p: If a question says 'in terms of electrons', an answer about oxygen scores zero.

core.h: Exam technique for redox in electrolysis
core.p: Most marks come from three linked statements: which ion goes to which electrode, whether it gains or loses electrons, and the name of the process.
bullets: Name the ion and its charge (e.g. 'positive copper ions, Cu2+').
Say where it goes and why: 'attracted to the negative cathode because opposite charges attract'.
State the electron change: 'each Cu2+ ion gains two electrons'.
Name the process: 'so the copper ions are reduced'.
For a full answer, do the same for the anode and say that the two processes happen together (redox).
Use the words **oxidised** and **reduced** for the species, and **oxidation** and **reduction** for the process.

callouts.t: Gain and lose must name electrons
callouts.p: Write 'gain electrons' not just 'gain'. Mark schemes need the word electrons.

analogy.t: A cash machine and a bank deposit
analogy.p: Think of electrons as money. At the **cathode** the power supply is paying out cash, so every positive ion that arrives is **given** money (gains electrons, **reduced**) - like collecting cash from a machine. At the **anode** the power supply is collecting cash, so every negative ion that arrives **pays in** its spare money (loses electrons, **oxidised**). The wire is the bank transfer that carries the money from the deposit point to the cash machine, so the money paid in always equals the money paid out. Where it breaks down: real money can be saved up, but electrons are not stored - they flow continuously, and ions only gain or lose a fixed number of electrons equal to their charge, not any amount they like.

terms.d: The loss of electrons.
The gain of electrons.
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction happen at the same time.
Describes a species that has lost electrons.
Describes a species that has gained electrons.
The decomposition of an electrolyte (an ionic compound that is molten or dissolved) using a direct current of electricity.
An ionic compound, molten or in aqueous solution, that conducts electricity because its ions can move.
The positive electrode in electrolysis, where oxidation occurs.
The negative electrode in electrolysis, where reduction occurs.
A positive ion, attracted to the cathode.
A negative ion, attracted to the anode.
An equation showing the reaction at one electrode, including the electrons gained or lost.
An electrode, such as graphite or platinum, that does not react during electrolysis.
When an ion gains or loses electrons at an electrode to become a neutral atom or molecule.
Memory aid: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).
Current that flows in one direction only, so one electrode stays positive and the other stays negative.

mistakes.w: Oxidation happens at the cathode.
mistakes.r: Oxidation happens at the anode; reduction happens at the cathode.

mistakes.w: Oxidation is gain of oxygen (when asked in terms of electrons).
mistakes.r: Oxidation is the loss of electrons.

mistakes.w: Positive ions go to the anode because the anode is positive.
mistakes.r: Positive ions are attracted to the negative cathode; opposite charges attract.

mistakes.w: Copper ions lose electrons at the cathode.
mistakes.r: Copper ions gain electrons at the cathode, so they are reduced: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu.

mistakes.w: Chloride ions are reduced to chlorine.
mistakes.r: Chloride ions lose electrons, so they are oxidised: 2Cl- → Cl2 + 2e-.

mistakes.w: Electrons flow through the electrolyte.
mistakes.r: Ions move through the electrolyte; electrons flow only through the external wires and electrodes.

mistakes.w: Cl- → Cl2 + e-
mistakes.r: Balance atoms and charge: 2Cl- → Cl2 + 2e-.

mistakes.w: Reduction is losing electrons because the charge is reduced.
mistakes.r: Reduction is gaining electrons; the positive charge decreases because negative electrons are added.

mistakes.w: The ions 'gain' at the cathode (no mention of electrons).
mistakes.r: State clearly that the ions gain electrons.

exam.q: State what is meant by oxidation, in terms of electrons.
model: Loss of electrons.
exam.tip: Must mention electrons.

exam.q: State at which electrode reduction occurs during electrolysis.
model: The cathode / the negative electrode.
exam.tip: RED CAT: reduction at cathode.

exam.q: The half equation at one electrode is Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu. Explain whether this is oxidation or reduction.
model: Reduction.
Because copper ions gain electrons.
exam.tip: Electrons on the left mean gained.

exam.q: During electrolysis of molten lead bromide, bromine forms at the anode. Write the half equation and explain why the bromide ions are oxidised.
model: Bromide ions lose electrons.
Loss of electrons is oxidation.
exam.tip: Remember Br2 is diatomic, so 2Br- and 2e-.

exam.q: Explain why electrolysis is described as a redox process.
model: Oxidation (loss of electrons) happens at the anode.
Reduction (gain of electrons) happens at the cathode at the same time.
exam.tip: Redox = both processes together.

exam.q: Molten sodium chloride is electrolysed. Explain, in terms of electrons, what happens at each electrode.
model: Na+ ions attracted to cathode / negative electrode.
Na+ ions gain an electron to form sodium: Na+ + e- → Na; this is reduction.
Cl- ions attracted to anode / positive electrode.
Cl- ions lose electrons to form chlorine: 2Cl- → Cl2 + 2e-; this is oxidation.
exam.tip: Give ion, electrode, electron change and process for each side.

exam.q: Identify the species that is oxidised in this reaction: 4OH- → O2 + 2H2O + 4e-. Give a reason.
model: Hydroxide ions (OH-).
They lose electrons.
exam.tip: Electrons appear as a product.

exam.q: A student says 'the anode is positive so positive ions are reduced there'. Explain two errors in this statement.
model: Positive ions are attracted to the cathode, not the anode (opposite charges attract).
Reduction happens at the cathode; oxidation happens at the anode.
exam.tip: Correct each error separately.

exam.q: During electrolysis of sodium chloride solution, hydrogen forms at the cathode. Write the half equation and state the type of reaction.
model: Reduction.
exam.tip: H2 is diatomic so 2H+ and 2e-.

exam.q: Explain how the electrons involved at the anode and cathode are linked in an electrolysis cell.
model: Anions lose electrons to the anode.
These electrons flow through the external circuit / via the power supply to the cathode.
At the cathode cations gain the same number of electrons, so electrons lost equals electrons gained.
exam.tip: Electrons move in the wires, ions in the electrolyte.

exam.q: Describe and explain, in terms of oxidation and reduction, what happens to the ions when molten lead bromide is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Include half equations.
model: The ionic compound is molten, so Pb2+ and Br- ions are free to move.
Pb2+ ions are attracted to the negative cathode.
Pb2+ + 2e- → Pb: lead ions gain electrons, so they are reduced; molten lead forms.
Br- ions are attracted to the positive anode.
2Br- → Br2 + 2e-: bromide ions lose electrons, so they are oxidised; brown bromine vapour forms.
Oxidation and reduction occur at the same time, so it is a redox reaction; electrons flow round the external circuit from anode to cathode.
exam.tip: Structure: ions free to move, then cathode, then anode, then link.

worked.q: For the electrolysis of molten aluminium oxide, Al3+ ions form aluminium at the cathode and O2- ions form oxygen at the anode. Write both half equations and state which is oxidation and which is reduction.
steps: Cathode: Al3+ needs 3 electrons to become a neutral atom: Al3+ + 3e- → Al.
Electrons are on the left, so they are gained: this is **reduction**.
Anode: oxygen is O2, so two oxide ions are needed: 2O2- → O2.
Charge on left is 4-, right is 0, so add 4e- to the right: 2O2- → O2 + 4e-.
Electrons are on the right, so they are lost: this is **oxidation**.
worked.ans: Cathode: Al3+ + 3e- → Al (reduction). Anode: 2O2- → O2 + 4e- (oxidation).

worked.q: Classify each as oxidation or reduction: (a) Zn2+ + 2e- → Zn (b) 2I- → I2 + 2e- (c) 2H+ + 2e- → H2, and say at which electrode each would happen.
steps: (a) Electrons gained by zinc ions → reduction → cathode.
(b) Electrons lost by iodide ions → oxidation → anode.
(c) Electrons gained by hydrogen ions → reduction → cathode.
worked.ans: (a) reduction, cathode; (b) oxidation, anode; (c) reduction, cathode.

worked.q: Combine the half equations for molten lead bromide to give the overall ionic equation.
steps: Cathode: Pb2+ + 2e- → Pb.
Anode: 2Br- → Br2 + 2e-.
Electrons lost (2) equal electrons gained (2), so add the equations.
Pb2+ + 2Br- + 2e- → Pb + Br2 + 2e-.
Cancel the electrons on both sides.
worked.ans: Pb2+ + 2Br- → Pb + Br2

chem_edx.3.13.summary: Copper is purified by electrolysis using an **impure copper anode**, a **pure copper cathode** and **copper sulfate solution** as the electrolyte. At the anode copper atoms are **oxidised** to Cu2+ ions (Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-) and go into solution, while at the cathode Cu2+ ions are **reduced** to copper atoms (Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu) that deposit as pure copper. The anode gets smaller, the cathode gets bigger, insoluble impurities fall to the bottom as **anode sludge**, and the copper sulfate concentration stays the same.

core.p: Copper extracted from its ores is not pure enough for many uses. Copper is used for **electrical wiring** because it is an excellent conductor and is ductile, but even small amounts of impurity **increase its resistance**, wasting energy as heat. Electrolysis can produce copper that is about 99.99% pure.
bullets: Impure copper typically contains other metals such as silver, gold, zinc and iron.
Impurities disrupt the regular arrangement of copper ions, so delocalised electrons cannot flow as easily: higher resistance.
Pure copper is needed for wires, electrical cables and electronics.
Electrolysis is the method used because it moves only copper from one electrode to the other.

callouts.p: Electrolysis with copper electrodes transfers copper from an impure anode to a pure cathode.

core.p: The cell is an electrolysis cell with **active (non-inert) copper electrodes**. The electrodes take part in the reaction, unlike graphite or platinum electrodes.
bullets: **Anode (positive electrode)**: a large block of **impure copper**.
**Cathode (negative electrode)**: a thin sheet of **pure copper**.
**Electrolyte**: **copper sulfate solution**, CuSO4(aq), which supplies Cu2+ ions (usually acidified with sulfuric acid in industry).
A **direct current (d.c.)** power supply is connected so the impure copper is positive.
Many anodes and cathodes are hung in large tanks in industry.

head: Part
Material
Charge
What happens
rows: Copper atoms lose electrons and dissolve
Copper ions gain electrons and deposit

callouts.t: Get them the right way round
callouts.p: Impure copper must be the anode. If it were the cathode, copper would deposit onto the impure block instead of leaving it.

fig.cap: Purifying copper. The impure copper anode dissolves, copper ions move through the copper sulfate solution and pure copper builds up on the cathode. Insoluble impurities collect under the anode as sludge.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><defs><marker id='pc1' markerWidth='8' markerHeight='8' refX='6' refY='3' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L6,3 L0,6 z' fill='#1b2540'/></marker></defs><rect x='90' y='80' width='220' height='130' fill='#dbeafe' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='2'/><polyline points='140,50 140,28 194,28' fill='none' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='2'/><polyline points='206,28 260,28 260,50' fill='none' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='194' y1='18' x2='194' y2='38' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='3'/><line x1='206' y1='22' x2='206' y2='34' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='125' y='50' width='30' height='140' fill='#b45309' stroke='#1b2540'/><rect x='255' y='50' width='10' height='140' fill='#f59e0b' stroke='#1b2540'/><rect x='110' y='196' width='60' height='12' fill='#78716c' stroke='#1b2540'/><text x='200' y='12' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1b2540'>d.c. supply</text><text x='118' y='44' font-size='12' text-anchor='end' fill='#b91c1c'>Impure anode (+)</text><text x='272' y='44' font-size='12' text-anchor='start' fill='#1d4ed8'>Pure cathode (-)</text><circle cx='200' cy='130' r='15' fill='#bfdbfe' stroke='#1d4ed8'/><text x='200' y='134' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1b2540'>Cu2+</text><line x1='217' y1='130' x2='246' y2='130' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#pc1)'/><line x1='160' y1='130' x2='182' y2='130' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#pc1)'/><text x='205' y='172' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1b2540'>CuSO4(aq)</text><text x='140' y='230' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#44403c'>Anode sludge</text><text x='290' y='230' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#b45309'>Copper deposits</text></svg>

core.p: The anode is connected to the positive terminal, which pulls electrons away from it. Copper atoms in the impure anode **lose two electrons each** and become Cu2+ ions, which dissolve into the solution. This is **oxidation** (loss of electrons).
bullets: Half equation: **Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-**
The copper anode **dissolves**, so it gets thinner and **loses mass**.
Here the anode itself reacts. Sulfate and hydroxide ions are **not** discharged, because copper atoms lose electrons more easily.
So **no oxygen gas** is given off at a copper anode (unlike with inert electrodes).
The electrons travel round the external circuit to the cathode.

callouts.p: Cu(s) → Cu2+(aq) + 2e-  (oxidation)

core.p: The cathode is connected to the negative terminal, which supplies electrons. Cu2+ ions in the solution are attracted to the negative cathode, where each **gains two electrons** and becomes a copper atom that sticks to the electrode. This is **reduction** (gain of electrons).
bullets: Half equation: **Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu**
A layer of **pure copper** builds up, so the cathode **gains mass**.
Copper ions are discharged rather than H+ ions because copper is **less reactive than hydrogen**.
Only copper deposits, which is why the cathode copper is pure.
The pinkish-brown copper coating can be seen growing on the cathode.

callouts.p: Cu2+(aq) + 2e- → Cu(s)  (reduction)

core.p: Not everything in the impure anode becomes copper on the cathode. Insoluble impurities simply fall off as the copper around them dissolves away.
bullets: Unreactive impurities such as **silver and gold** do not dissolve; they fall to the bottom of the cell as **anode sludge** (anode mud).
Anode sludge can be collected and processed because it contains **valuable metals**, which helps make the process economic.
Some more reactive metal impurities may dissolve as ions but stay in solution; they are **not deposited** at the cathode.
So the anode loses **more mass** than the cathode gains, because the anode also loses impurities.

callouts.p: Say 'impurities fall to the bottom as anode sludge'. Mark schemes reward 'sludge' or 'collect below the anode'.

core.h: Changes in mass of the electrodes
core.p: The mass changes are the clearest evidence of what is happening. Copper is transferred from the anode to the cathode.
bullets: Anode: mass **decreases** (copper dissolves, impurities drop off).
Cathode: mass **increases** (pure copper deposited).
If both electrodes were pure copper, the mass lost by the anode would **equal** the mass gained by the cathode.
With an impure anode, mass lost by anode > mass gained by cathode; the difference is mostly the sludge.
Mass of copper deposited increases with **larger current** and **longer time** (more electrons transferred).

fig.cap: Before and after purification. The impure anode becomes thinner while the pure cathode becomes thicker as copper is transferred across.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><defs><marker id='pc2' markerWidth='8' markerHeight='8' refX='6' refY='3' orient='auto'><path d='M0,0 L6,3 L0,6 z' fill='#1b2540'/></marker></defs><text x='100' y='24' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1b2540'>Start</text><text x='290' y='24' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1b2540'>After electrolysis</text><rect x='50' y='40' width='40' height='140' fill='#b45309' stroke='#1b2540'/><rect x='130' y='40' width='8' height='140' fill='#f59e0b' stroke='#1b2540'/><line x1='165' y1='110' x2='215' y2='110' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#pc2)'/><rect x='240' y='40' width='18' height='140' fill='#b45309' stroke='#1b2540'/><rect x='320' y='40' width='26' height='140' fill='#f59e0b' stroke='#1b2540'/><text x='70' y='198' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#b91c1c'>anode</text><text x='134' y='198' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1d4ed8'>cathode</text><text x='249' y='198' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#b91c1c'>anode</text><text x='333' y='198' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1d4ed8'>cathode</text><text x='290' y='218' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#b91c1c'>anode loses mass</text><text x='290' y='234' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1d4ed8'>cathode gains mass</text></svg>

core.h: Why the electrolyte concentration stays constant
core.p: For every Cu2+ ion that leaves the solution at the cathode, one Cu2+ ion enters the solution at the anode. The two half equations involve the **same number of electrons**, so the rates match.
bullets: Anode adds Cu2+: Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-.
Cathode removes Cu2+: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu.
Net change in Cu2+ in solution: **zero**.
So the **blue colour** of the copper sulfate solution **stays the same**.
Compare inert electrodes: Cu2+ is removed but not replaced, so the blue colour **fades**.

callouts.p: With copper electrodes the solution stays blue because copper ions are removed at the cathode at the same rate as they are added at the anode.

core.p: The electrode material changes the anode product. With inert electrodes the anode cannot dissolve, so something in the solution must be oxidised instead.
bullets: Cathode product is copper in both cases.
Copper anode: copper atoms are oxidised and dissolve.
Inert (graphite) anode: hydroxide ions are oxidised and oxygen bubbles off: 4OH- → O2 + 2H2O + 4e-.
With inert electrodes the solution becomes **paler** and more **acidic** (H+ and SO4 2- remain).
Only the copper-electrode cell is used for purification.

core.h: The whole process as a flow of copper
core.p: It helps to follow a single copper atom. It starts in the impure anode, loses two electrons to become an ion, drifts through the solution towards the cathode, gains two electrons and becomes part of the pure copper.
bullets: Step 1: Cu atom in anode loses 2e- (oxidation).
Step 2: Cu2+ ion moves through the electrolyte towards the negative cathode.
Step 3: Cu2+ gains 2e- at the cathode (reduction).
Step 4: Cu atom joins the pure copper layer.
Impurity atoms do not follow this route: they become sludge or stay in solution.

fig.cap: Route of copper through the cell. Copper is oxidised at the anode and reduced at the cathode; impurities end up as sludge, and the copper ion concentration does not change.

core.p: Purification is a redox process: oxidation at the anode and reduction at the cathode happen together, linked by electrons flowing through the external circuit.
bullets: Electrons lost at anode (2 per Cu) = electrons gained at cathode (2 per Cu2+).
Overall there is **no chemical change**: Cu(impure) → Cu(pure).
The energy from the power supply is used to move copper, not to make a new substance.
A larger current moves more electrons per second, so copper transfers faster.

core.p: Questions usually ask you to explain the set-up, give the half equations, and explain an observation (mass change, colour, sludge). Link each observation to its reason.
bullets: Always name both electrodes with their material **and** charge.
Give half equations with correct charges and 2e-.
Use 'oxidised' for copper atoms at the anode and 'reduced' for copper ions at the cathode.
Explain the constant colour by comparing the rates of Cu2+ added and removed.
Explain the difference in mass changes using impurities/sludge.

callouts.p: Half equations are Higher tier. Foundation answers can still score by saying 'copper atoms lose electrons at the anode' and 'copper ions gain electrons at the cathode'.

analogy.p: Imagine an old, messy wall (the impure anode) mixed with rubble. Workers (the electric current) pull out only the good bricks (copper atoms), carry them across a river as parcels (Cu2+ ions in solution) and rebuild them into a perfect new wall (the pure cathode). The rubble they do not want simply falls in a heap at the foot of the old wall (anode sludge). The river always holds the same number of parcels because one goes in as one comes out (constant concentration). Where it breaks down: real bricks keep their shape, but copper atoms change into ions and back again by losing and gaining electrons, and the workers do not choose - copper is moved simply because of the electrode charges and how easily copper loses and gains electrons.

terms.d: Using electrolysis with an impure copper anode, pure copper cathode and copper sulfate solution to produce very pure copper.
The positive electrode, made of the copper to be purified; it dissolves during electrolysis.
The negative electrode, a thin sheet of pure copper on which pure copper is deposited.
The electrolyte, CuSO4(aq), which provides Cu2+ ions to carry charge between the electrodes.
Insoluble impurities (such as silver and gold) that fall to the bottom of the cell beneath the anode.
An electrode that takes part in the electrolysis reaction, such as a copper anode that dissolves.
An electrode, such as graphite or platinum, that does not react during electrolysis.
The loss of electrons; at the anode Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-.
The gain of electrons; at the cathode Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu.
The positive electrode, where oxidation happens.
The negative electrode, where reduction happens.
Decomposition of an electrolyte using a direct current; here used to transfer copper between electrodes.
Current flowing in one direction so the anode stays positive and the cathode stays negative.
An equation showing the electrons gained or lost at one electrode.
Opposition to current; impurities in copper increase it, which is why pure copper is needed for wires.

mistakes.w: The pure copper is the anode.
mistakes.r: Impure copper is the anode (positive); pure copper is the cathode (negative).

mistakes.w: Oxygen is given off at the anode.
mistakes.r: With a copper anode, copper atoms are oxidised and dissolve: Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-; no oxygen forms.

mistakes.w: Cu2+ → Cu + 2e- at the cathode.
mistakes.r: Electrons are gained at the cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu.

mistakes.w: The blue colour fades because copper ions are used up.
mistakes.r: The colour stays the same because Cu2+ ions are added at the anode at the same rate they are removed at the cathode.

mistakes.w: The impurities are deposited on the cathode.
mistakes.r: Impurities fall as anode sludge or stay in solution; only copper is deposited at the cathode.

mistakes.w: The anode loses the same mass as the cathode gains.
mistakes.r: The anode loses more mass because impurities also leave it as sludge.

mistakes.w: Copper ions are oxidised at the cathode.
mistakes.r: Copper ions gain electrons, so they are reduced at the cathode.

mistakes.w: Copper is purified because electrolysis removes oxygen.
mistakes.r: Copper atoms are transferred from anode to cathode as ions; impurities are left behind.

exam.q: Name the electrolyte used in the purification of copper.
model: Copper sulfate solution.
exam.tip: Accept CuSO4(aq).

exam.q: State what the anode is made of in the purification of copper.
model: Impure copper.
exam.tip: Impure at the anode, pure at the cathode.

exam.q: Write the half equation for the reaction at the anode.
model: Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-
exam.tip: Electrons on the right for oxidation.

exam.q: Write the half equation for the reaction at the cathode and state whether it is oxidation or reduction.
model: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu
Reduction (gain of electrons).
exam.tip: RED CAT.

exam.q: Explain why the mass of the anode decreases during purification.
model: Copper atoms lose electrons / are oxidised to Cu2+ ions.
The ions dissolve into the solution (and impurities fall off).
exam.tip: Mention ions going into solution.

exam.q: Explain why the blue colour of the copper sulfate solution does not change.
model: Cu2+ ions are removed at the cathode.
Cu2+ ions are produced at the anode at the same rate, so concentration stays constant.
exam.tip: Rates or amounts must be equal.

exam.q: Explain why the decrease in mass of the anode is greater than the increase in mass of the cathode.
model: The anode contains impurities.
Impurities fall to the bottom as sludge / are not deposited on the cathode.
exam.tip: Link difference in mass to impurities.

exam.q: Explain why copper used for electrical wiring needs to be very pure.
model: Impurities increase the resistance of the copper.
So pure copper conducts electricity better / less energy is wasted.
exam.tip: Mention resistance or conductivity.

exam.q: Compare the anode reactions when copper sulfate solution is electrolysed with copper electrodes and with graphite electrodes.
model: Copper anode: copper atoms lose electrons / are oxidised.
Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-, so the anode dissolves and loses mass.
Graphite anode: hydroxide ions lose electrons / are oxidised.
4OH- → O2 + 2H2O + 4e-, so oxygen bubbles form and the anode mass does not change.
exam.tip: Give a matching point for each electrode type.

exam.q: Describe and explain how copper is purified by electrolysis. Include the electrodes, electrolyte, reactions and what happens to the impurities.
model: Impure copper is the anode (positive) and pure copper is the cathode (negative); electrolyte is copper sulfate solution; d.c. supply.
At the anode copper atoms lose electrons: Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-; this is oxidation.
The anode dissolves and gets smaller.
Cu2+ ions move to the negative cathode and gain electrons: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu; this is reduction.
Pure copper is deposited so the cathode gets bigger.
Impurities fall to the bottom as anode sludge (and may contain valuable metals); Cu2+ concentration stays constant.
exam.tip: Cover set-up, anode, cathode and impurities in that order.

worked.q: In a purification cell the impure anode starts at 52.0 g and ends at 40.4 g. The pure cathode starts at 10.0 g and ends at 21.1 g. Calculate the mass of impurities released from the anode and the percentage purity of the copper removed from the anode.
steps: Mass lost by anode = 52.0 - 40.4 = 11.6 g.
Mass gained by cathode = 21.1 - 10.0 = 11.1 g (this is pure copper).
Mass of impurities = 11.6 - 11.1 = 0.5 g.
Percentage of copper in the material lost = (11.1 / 11.6) x 100 = 95.7%.
worked.ans: 0.5 g of impurities; the impure copper that dissolved was about 95.7% copper.

worked.q: A student uses two pure copper electrodes in copper sulfate solution. After 30 minutes the cathode has gained 0.64 g. Predict the mass change of the anode and the colour change of the solution. Explain.
steps: Both electrodes are pure copper, so no sludge forms.
Every copper atom lost from the anode becomes an ion that replaces one deposited at the cathode.
So the anode loses the same mass as the cathode gains: 0.64 g.
Cu2+ is added and removed at the same rate, so the concentration does not change.
worked.ans: Anode loses 0.64 g; the solution stays the same blue colour.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why silver impurities are found in the anode sludge but zinc impurities are not.
steps: Silver is less reactive than copper, so silver atoms do not lose electrons at the anode.
As the copper around them dissolves, silver atoms are released and fall to the bottom as sludge.
Zinc is more reactive than copper, so zinc atoms lose electrons and dissolve as Zn2+ ions.
Zn2+ ions stay in solution and are not deposited at the cathode because copper ions are discharged instead.
worked.ans: Unreactive silver does not dissolve and forms sludge; reactive zinc dissolves as ions that remain in the solution.

chem_edx.3.14.summary: In this core practical you electrolyse **copper sulfate solution** twice: with **inert (graphite) electrodes** and with **copper electrodes**. With inert electrodes copper is deposited on the cathode, **oxygen** bubbles off at the anode and the blue colour fades; with copper electrodes the **anode loses mass**, the **cathode gains the same mass** and the solution stays blue. The quantitative part measures the **change in mass of copper electrodes** at different **currents** for a fixed time, showing that mass of copper deposited is proportional to current.

core.p: The aim is to investigate what happens when copper sulfate solution is electrolysed with **inert electrodes** and with **copper electrodes**, and to find how the **mass change of copper electrodes** depends on the **current**. It brings together electrode products, half equations, and oxidation and reduction.
bullets: Part 1 (qualitative): graphite electrodes; observe products at each electrode.
Part 2 (quantitative): copper electrodes; measure mass changes for different currents.
Electrolyte: aqueous copper sulfate, CuSO4(aq), containing Cu2+, SO4 2-, H+ and OH- ions.
Power supply must be **direct current (d.c.)**.

callouts.p: You can be asked to describe the method, name variables, process results, draw a graph and evaluate errors.

core.p: The electrodes are connected in series with a d.c. power pack, an **ammeter** to measure the current and a **variable resistor** to adjust and keep the current constant.
bullets: Beaker of copper sulfate solution (e.g. 0.5 mol/dm3).
Two graphite rods (part 1) or two strips of copper foil (part 2).
Low-voltage d.c. power pack, connecting leads and crocodile clips.
Ammeter and variable resistor (rheostat).
Stopclock, top-pan balance (at least 0.01 g resolution).
Emery paper / sandpaper, distilled water, propanone (optional) and a drying method.
Wooden splint (to test oxygen).

fig.cap: Apparatus for electrolysing copper sulfate solution. The ammeter (A) measures the current and the variable resistor is adjusted to keep it constant.

core.p: With graphite electrodes the electrodes do not react, so the products come from ions in the solution.
bullets: Pour copper sulfate solution into a beaker and place two clean graphite rods in it, not touching.
Connect the rods to a d.c. power pack (about 4 V) and switch on.
Observe each electrode for a few minutes.
Collect the gas at the anode in an inverted test tube filled with solution, then test with a **glowing splint**.
Note any colour change of the solution after a longer run.

core.h: Results and explanation with inert electrodes
core.p: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so Cu2+ ions are discharged at the cathode instead of H+. There are no halide ions, so OH- ions are discharged at the anode instead of sulfate ions.
bullets: Cathode (-): **pink-brown copper** coats the electrode. Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu (**reduction**).
Anode (+): **bubbles of colourless gas**; oxygen **relights a glowing splint**. 4OH- → O2 + 2H2O + 4e- (**oxidation**).
Solution: **blue colour fades** because Cu2+ ions are removed and not replaced.
Solution becomes more **acidic**: H+ and SO4 2- ions are left behind (sulfuric acid forms).
Graphite anode mass does not change.

callouts.p: Oxygen relights a glowing splint. Do not confuse with hydrogen (squeaky pop with a lit splint).

fig.cap: Inert graphite electrodes. Oxygen bubbles form at the anode, copper coats the cathode and the blue colour gradually fades as Cu2+ ions are used up.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 240' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='100' y='80' width='200' height='130' fill='#e0f2fe' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='2'/><polyline points='147,50 147,28 194,28' fill='none' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='2'/><polyline points='206,28 253,28 253,50' fill='none' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='194' y1='18' x2='194' y2='38' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='3'/><line x1='206' y1='22' x2='206' y2='34' stroke='#1b2540' stroke-width='3'/><rect x='140' y='50' width='14' height='140' fill='#374151' stroke='#1b2540'/><rect x='246' y='50' width='14' height='140' fill='#374151' stroke='#1b2540'/><rect x='243' y='110' width='20' height='80' fill='#c2410c' stroke='#7c2d12'/><circle cx='162' cy='170' r='3' fill='#ffffff' stroke='#1b2540'/><circle cx='166' cy='150' r='4' fill='#ffffff' stroke='#1b2540'/><circle cx='161' cy='128' r='3' fill='#ffffff' stroke='#1b2540'/><circle cx='167' cy='106' r='4' fill='#ffffff' stroke='#1b2540'/><circle cx='162' cy='88' r='3' fill='#ffffff' stroke='#1b2540'/><text x='200' y='12' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1b2540'>d.c. supply</text><text x='132' y='44' font-size='12' text-anchor='end' fill='#b91c1c'>Anode (+)</text><text x='268' y='44' font-size='12' text-anchor='start' fill='#1d4ed8'>Cathode (-)</text><text x='205' y='200' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1b2540'>Blue fades</text><text x='120' y='230' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#1b2540'>Oxygen bubbles</text><text x='290' y='230' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='#c2410c'>Copper coating</text></svg>

core.h: Method part 2: copper electrodes and current
core.p: This part measures how the **mass change** of the electrodes depends on the **current**. Each run uses fresh, cleaned and weighed copper electrodes.
bullets: Clean two copper strips with **emery paper** to remove oxide and grease, so copper deposits evenly.
Label the strips anode and cathode, then weigh each on a balance and record the mass.
Place them in copper sulfate solution, not touching, and connect them in the circuit with the ammeter and variable resistor.
Switch on and adjust the variable resistor to the chosen current (e.g. 0.2 A); start the stopclock.
Keep the current constant by adjusting the variable resistor; run for a fixed time (e.g. 20 minutes).
Switch off, carefully remove the electrodes, rinse gently with **distilled water** (then dip in propanone), and **dry** them.
Reweigh each electrode and calculate the change in mass.
Repeat with fresh electrodes at other currents (e.g. 0.3, 0.4, 0.5 A).

callouts.p: Freshly deposited copper is loosely attached. Rubbing or rinsing hard can knock it off and make the mass gain too low.

core.h: Results and explanation with copper electrodes
core.p: With copper electrodes the copper anode is oxidised itself, because copper atoms lose electrons more easily than OH- ions. Copper is moved from anode to cathode.
bullets: Anode (+): Cu → Cu2+ + 2e- (**oxidation**); the anode **loses mass**; no gas forms.
Cathode (-): Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu (**reduction**); the cathode **gains mass**.
Mass lost by anode ≈ mass gained by cathode (both pure copper).
The blue colour stays the same: Cu2+ is added at the anode at the same rate it is removed at the cathode.
Larger current = more electrons per second = more copper transferred in the same time.

core.p: A fair test changes only the independent variable.
bullets: **Independent variable**: current (A).
**Dependent variable**: change in mass of the electrodes (g).

**Control variables**: time of electrolysis, concentration and volume of copper sulfate solution, size (surface area) of electrodes, distance between electrodes, depth electrodes are dipped, temperature.
The variable resistor is what lets you set and hold the current.

callouts.p: Mass of copper depends on the total charge passed, which depends on both current and time. To see the effect of current alone, time must be the same.

core.p: Calculate each mass change (final - initial). A gain is positive, a loss is negative. Plot mass change (y-axis) against current (x-axis) for both electrodes.
bullets: Cathode points lie on a **straight line through the origin**: mass gained is **directly proportional** to current.
Anode points give a mirror-image line below the axis: mass lost is proportional to current.
Doubling the current doubles the mass change (for the same time).
Identify anomalous results as points far from the line of best fit and exclude them from means.
Repeat each current and calculate a mean to improve reliability.

fig.cap: Typical results. The cathode gain and the anode loss are both directly proportional to the current for a fixed time, giving straight lines through the origin.

core.p: Most errors make the measured mass changes wrong, especially the cathode gain.
bullets: Copper **flakes off** the cathode when removed or rinsed: cathode gain too small. Handle gently; rinse by dipping, not rubbing.
Electrodes **not fully dry** when reweighed: masses too high. Dry thoroughly (propanone evaporates quickly) before weighing.
Current **drifts** during the run: adjust the variable resistor continuously.
Electrodes not cleaned: copper deposit is uneven or does not stick; oxide layer affects mass.
Balance resolution too low for small mass changes: use a balance reading to 0.01 g or better, or run for longer.
Electrodes touching: short circuit, no electrolysis.

callouts.p: If the anode loses slightly more than the cathode gains, copper may have fallen off the anode or cathode into the beaker.

core.p: The risks are low but must be controlled.
bullets: Copper sulfate solution is **harmful/irritant**: wear **eye protection** and avoid skin contact.
Propanone is **highly flammable**: keep away from flames.
Use a **low voltage** d.c. supply; do not let electrodes touch (short circuit, heating).
Wash hands after the practical; dispose of copper sulfate as instructed, not down the sink.

core.p: Every result is explained by OIL RIG: oxidation (loss of electrons) at the anode and reduction (gain of electrons) at the cathode.
bullets: Inert anode: OH- ions are oxidised to oxygen.
Copper anode: copper atoms are oxidised to Cu2+ ions.
Both set-ups: Cu2+ ions are reduced to copper at the cathode.
Electrons lost at the anode = electrons gained at the cathode, which is why the masses match with copper electrodes.
This experiment models the industrial **purification of copper**.

callouts.p: Writing and balancing the half equations is Higher tier; all students should describe the observations and name the products.

analogy.p: With copper electrodes the cell is like a conveyor belt: copper is taken off one stack (the anode), carried across as ions, and stacked on the other side (the cathode). Turning up the speed of the belt (the current) moves more copper in the same time, which is why mass change is proportional to current. With graphite electrodes there is no stack to take from, so the belt only unloads copper that was already in the solution, and the supply runs down (the blue fades) while oxygen is made at the other end instead. Where it breaks down: a conveyor carries the same objects, but copper atoms change into ions and back by losing and gaining electrons, and the 'belt' is really electrons moving through the wire while ions move through the solution.

terms.d: The decomposition of an electrolyte using a direct current of electricity.
An ionic compound, molten or dissolved, that conducts electricity because its ions can move.
An electrode, such as graphite or platinum, that does not react during electrolysis.
An active electrode that takes part in the reaction; a copper anode dissolves.
The positive electrode, where oxidation happens.
The negative electrode, where reduction happens.
The loss of electrons.
The gain of electrons.
Meter connected in series to measure the current in amperes (A).
A component used to adjust the resistance and so set and keep the current constant.
The variable deliberately changed; here, the current.
The variable measured; here, the change in mass of the electrodes.
A variable kept the same so the test is fair, e.g. time, concentration and electrode size.
When one quantity doubles the other doubles; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
Test for oxygen: a glowing splint relights.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the others, often due to an error.

mistakes.w: Hydrogen is produced at the cathode with copper sulfate solution.
mistakes.r: Copper is produced at the cathode because copper is less reactive than hydrogen.

mistakes.w: Sulfur dioxide or sulfur is produced at the anode.
mistakes.r: With inert electrodes oxygen is produced from hydroxide ions; sulfate ions are not discharged.

mistakes.w: With copper electrodes oxygen bubbles form at the anode.
mistakes.r: With copper electrodes the anode dissolves (Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-) and no gas forms.

mistakes.w: The independent variable is the mass of copper.
mistakes.r: The independent variable is the current; mass change is the dependent variable.

mistakes.w: Test oxygen with a lit splint - it pops.
mistakes.r: Oxygen relights a glowing splint; a squeaky pop is the test for hydrogen.

mistakes.w: Weigh the electrodes straight after taking them out.
mistakes.r: Rinse with distilled water and dry them before reweighing, otherwise the mass is too high.

mistakes.w: The solution stays blue with graphite electrodes.
mistakes.r: With graphite electrodes the blue fades as Cu2+ ions are removed; it stays blue only with copper electrodes.

mistakes.w: Mass increase is proportional to voltage.
mistakes.r: In this practical the current is measured and controlled; mass change is proportional to current (for fixed time).

mistakes.w: Use an alternating current supply.
mistakes.r: A direct current (d.c.) supply is needed so each electrode keeps its charge.

exam.q: Name the product formed at the cathode when copper sulfate solution is electrolysed with graphite electrodes.
model: Copper.
exam.tip: Copper is less reactive than hydrogen.

exam.q: Describe the test for the gas formed at the anode when copper sulfate solution is electrolysed with graphite electrodes.
model: Insert a glowing splint.
It relights (oxygen).
exam.tip: Glowing, not lit.

exam.q: State the independent and dependent variables in the investigation of current and mass change.
model: Independent: current.
Dependent: change in mass of the electrode(s).
exam.tip: Independent is what you change.

exam.q: Give two control variables in this investigation.
model: Any two from: time; concentration of copper sulfate; volume of solution; size/surface area of electrodes; distance between electrodes; temperature.
exam.tip: Avoid vague answers like 'same equipment'.

exam.q: Explain why the electrodes should be washed and dried before reweighing.
model: To remove copper sulfate solution / water.
Otherwise the measured mass would be too high.
exam.tip: Say the direction of the error.

exam.q: Explain why the blue colour fades with graphite electrodes but not with copper electrodes.
model: Blue colour is due to Cu2+ ions.
With graphite, Cu2+ ions are removed at the cathode and not replaced, so the colour fades.
With copper electrodes, Cu2+ ions are produced at the anode at the same rate as removed at the cathode, so concentration stays the same.
exam.tip: Name Cu2+ as the cause of the blue.

exam.q: Write the half equations for the reactions at each electrode when copper sulfate solution is electrolysed with copper electrodes.
model: Anode: Cu → Cu2+ + 2e-
Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu
exam.tip: Same species, opposite directions.

exam.q: A student found the cathode gained less mass than the anode lost. Suggest two reasons.
model: Some copper fell off the cathode (when removed or rinsed).
Cathode / anode not dried properly, or copper fell off the anode into the beaker.
exam.tip: Think about what happens when handling the electrodes.

exam.q: Explain why the variable resistor is needed in the circuit.
model: To adjust the current to the chosen value.
To keep the current constant during the experiment.
exam.tip: Constant current is needed for a fair test.

exam.q: Describe how to investigate the effect of current on the mass of copper deposited at the cathode during the electrolysis of copper sulfate solution. Include how you would make the results valid.
model: Clean copper electrodes with emery paper and weigh them.
Place in copper sulfate solution and connect to a d.c. supply with an ammeter and variable resistor in series.
Set the current with the variable resistor and keep it constant; run for a fixed time measured with a stopclock.
Remove electrodes, rinse with distilled water, dry and reweigh; calculate mass change.
Repeat with new electrodes at different currents.
Control time, concentration, volume, electrode size and distance; repeat each current and calculate a mean.
exam.tip: Order your steps; mention the measuring instruments.

worked.q: A copper cathode had a mass of 12.46 g before and 12.83 g after electrolysis at 0.40 A for 30 minutes. Calculate the mass gained and predict the mass gained at 0.80 A for 30 minutes.
steps: Mass gained is directly proportional to current (time fixed).
0.80 A is double 0.40 A, so mass gained doubles.
Predicted mass gained = 2 x 0.37 = 0.74 g.
worked.ans: 0.37 g at 0.40 A; about 0.74 g at 0.80 A.

worked.q: Results for the cathode: 0.10 A: 0.09 g; 0.20 A: 0.19 g; 0.30 A: 0.36 g; 0.40 A: 0.38 g. Identify the anomalous result and describe the relationship.
steps: The pattern is roughly 0.095 g per 0.10 A.
Expected at 0.30 A is about 0.28-0.29 g, but 0.36 g was recorded.
So 0.30 A (0.36 g) is anomalous - possibly the electrode was not dry.
The other points show mass gained increases in proportion to current.
worked.ans: 0.36 g at 0.30 A is anomalous; mass gained is directly proportional to current.

worked.q: Model answer: describe and explain the observations when copper sulfate solution is electrolysed with graphite electrodes.
steps: At the cathode a pink-brown coating forms: Cu2+ ions gain electrons (reduction), Cu2+ + 2e- → Cu; copper is discharged because it is less reactive than hydrogen.
At the anode bubbles form that relight a glowing splint: OH- ions lose electrons (oxidation), 4OH- → O2 + 2H2O + 4e-.
The blue colour fades because Cu2+ ions are removed and not replaced.
The solution becomes acidic because H+ and SO4 2- ions remain.
worked.ans: Copper at the cathode, oxygen at the anode, blue colour fades and solution becomes acidic.

chem_edx.3.2.summary: Two completely separate ideas describe an acid. **Dilute and concentrated** describe the **amount of acid (solute) dissolved in a given volume of solution** - how much acid there is per dm3. **Strong and weak** describe the **degree of dissociation into ions** - what fraction of the acid molecules split up to release H+ ions in water. Strong acids such as hydrochloric, nitric and sulfuric acid are **fully dissociated**, while weak acids such as ethanoic, citric and carbonic acid are only **partially dissociated** in a reversible reaction, so at the same concentration a strong acid has a higher H+ concentration, a lower pH and reacts faster.

core.h: Two different questions about an acid
core.p: In everyday language 'strong' and 'concentrated' sound the same, but in chemistry they answer different questions. Getting these two pairs of words mixed up is one of the most common ways to lose marks in Topic 3.
bullets: **Concentrated or dilute?** asks: how much acid is dissolved in each dm3 of solution?
**Strong or weak?** asks: what proportion of the acid molecules have dissociated (split) into ions?
Concentration can be changed by adding water or more acid; strength cannot - it is a property of the acid itself
Any acid can be made concentrated or dilute, so you can have a **concentrated weak acid** or a **dilute strong acid**
The pH of a solution depends on **both**: how much acid is present and how much of it has dissociated

head: Pair of terms
Describes
Can you change it by adding water?
rows: Amount of acid per volume of solution
No - it depends on which acid it is

callouts.p: Concentration = amount of substance in a volume. Strength = degree of dissociation. They are independent of each other.

core.p: A **concentrated** solution has a **large amount of solute in a given volume** of solution; a **dilute** solution has a **small amount of solute in a given volume**. For acids, the solute is the acid, and the solvent is water.
bullets: Concentrated acid: lots of acid particles per dm3 of solution
Dilute acid: few acid particles per dm3 of solution
Adding water to an acid **dilutes** it: the same amount of acid is spread through a larger volume
Evaporating water or adding more acid makes a solution **more concentrated**
'Dilute' and 'concentrated' are relative terms - 1 mol/dm3 is concentrated compared with 0.1 mol/dm3 but dilute compared with 10 mol/dm3
These words are used for any solution, not just acids (e.g. a concentrated salt solution)

callouts.p: A solution with a large amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution (solvent).
A solution with a small amount of solute dissolved in a given volume of solution (solvent).

fig.cap: A dilute and a concentrated solution of the same acid. The red circles represent acid particles; the concentrated solution has many more acid particles in the same volume of water.

core.p: To compare 'dilute' and 'concentrated' properly, chemists give a number: the amount of solute per volume of solution. Volume is measured in dm3 (1 dm3 = 1000 cm3).
bullets: **Concentration in g/dm3 = mass of solute (g) / volume of solution (dm3)**
**(Higher) Concentration in mol/dm3 = amount of solute (mol) / volume of solution (dm3)**
Convert cm3 to dm3 by dividing by 1000
Doubling the volume by adding water halves the concentration (same amount of solute in twice the volume)
Two solutions with the same concentration in mol/dm3 contain the same number of acid formula units per dm3, which makes them a fair comparison of strength

callouts.p: Always state the unit: g/dm3 or mol/dm3 (also written g dm-3 or mol dm-3). A number without a unit usually loses the final mark.

core.p: When a **strong acid** dissolves in water, **all** (or virtually all) of its molecules **dissociate** (ionise) into ions. None of the original acid molecules are left. The reaction goes one way only, so a single arrow is used.
bullets: **Hydrochloric acid**: HCl(aq) → H+(aq) + Cl-(aq)
**Nitric acid**: HNO3(aq) → H+(aq) + NO3-(aq)
**Sulfuric acid**: H2SO4(aq) → 2H+(aq) + SO4 2-(aq)
Because every molecule releases its H+, strong acids give the **highest possible H+ concentration** for their concentration
So a strong acid has a **low pH** (e.g. 0.1 mol/dm3 HCl has pH 1)
Strong acids conduct electricity well because their solutions contain many ions

callouts.p: An acid that is completely (fully) dissociated into ions in aqueous solution.

fig.cap: Two acid solutions of the same concentration. In the strong acid (HCl) every molecule has dissociated into H+ and Cl- ions. In the weak acid most particles stay as undissociated molecules (HA) and only a few have formed H+ and A- ions, so the H+ concentration is much lower.

core.p: When a **weak acid** dissolves in water, only a **small fraction** of its molecules dissociate into ions - most stay as whole molecules. The dissociation is **reversible**: ions are constantly re-forming molecules while other molecules split, so the symbol ⇌ is used.
bullets: **Ethanoic acid** (vinegar): CH3COOH(aq) ⇌ CH3COO-(aq) + H+(aq)
**Citric acid** (citrus fruits) and **carbonic acid** (fizzy drinks, H2CO3) are also weak acids
In dilute ethanoic acid only around 1 molecule in 100 is dissociated at any moment
Because few H+ ions are released, a weak acid has a **higher pH** than a strong acid of the **same concentration** (e.g. 0.1 mol/dm3 ethanoic acid is about pH 3)
Weak acids conduct electricity less well than strong acids of the same concentration (fewer ions)
The undissociated molecules are a 'reserve' of acid: if H+ ions are used up in a reaction, more molecules dissociate to replace them

callouts.p: An acid that is only partially dissociated into ions in aqueous solution.
For a weak acid use the reversible arrow ⇌. For a strong acid use a single arrow →. Examiners notice.

core.p: The table below summarises the differences when a strong and a weak acid are compared **at the same concentration and temperature** - the only fair way to compare them.
bullets: Same concentration means the same amount of acid per dm3, so any difference must be due to strength
Higher H+ concentration in the strong acid → lower pH, faster reactions, better conductivity
Both still show all typical acid reactions (with metals, bases and carbonates) and form the same salts

callouts.p: Only compare strength at the same concentration. A concentrated weak acid can have a lower pH than a very dilute strong acid.

core.p: Reaction rate depends on collisions. In a reaction of an acid with a metal or carbonate, it is the **H+ ions** that react, so the rate depends on the **concentration of H+ ions**, not just on the concentration of the acid.
bullets: A strong acid has more H+ ions per unit volume than a weak acid of the same concentration
So there are **more frequent collisions** between H+ ions and the magnesium (or calcium carbonate) surface
So the strong acid reacts faster: more bubbles per second and the metal disappears sooner
But if the same amount (moles) of a monoprotic acid is used up completely, the **total volume of gas is the same**
This is because as H+ ions are used up in the weak acid, more molecules dissociate, until all the acid has reacted
So strength affects the **rate**, but not the **total amount** of product when the acid is the limiting reactant

callouts.p: Say 'higher concentration of H+ ions so more frequent collisions', not just 'stronger so faster'.

fig.cap: Volume of hydrogen against time when excess magnesium reacts with equal volumes of 1 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid (strong) and 1 mol/dm3 ethanoic acid (weak). The strong acid's curve is steeper (faster rate), but both finish at the same total volume because they contain the same amount of acid.

core.p: Because strength and concentration are independent, every acid solution can be described with one word from each pair. This lets you describe any acid precisely.
bullets: **Concentrated strong acid**: lots of acid per dm3, all dissociated - very low pH (e.g. 2 mol/dm3 HCl)
**Dilute strong acid**: little acid per dm3, all dissociated (e.g. 0.01 mol/dm3 HCl, pH 2)
**Concentrated weak acid**: lots of acid per dm3, only partly dissociated (e.g. glacial or 5 mol/dm3 ethanoic acid)
**Dilute weak acid**: little acid per dm3, only partly dissociated (e.g. vinegar is a dilute solution of ethanoic acid)
A dilute strong acid and a concentrated weak acid can have similar pH values, because both factors affect the H+ concentration

core.h: Linking strength and concentration to pH
core.p: The pH depends only on the concentration of H+ ions. That H+ concentration is set by two things together: how much acid is dissolved (concentration) and what fraction of it dissociates (strength).
bullets: Increasing concentration of any acid increases [H+] → pH decreases
Changing to a stronger acid at the same concentration increases [H+] → pH decreases
(Higher) Diluting a strong acid by a factor of 10 decreases [H+] by a factor of 10, so the pH increases by 1
(Higher) 0.1 mol/dm3 HCl has pH 1; 0.01 mol/dm3 HCl has pH 2; 0.001 mol/dm3 has pH 3
A weak acid at the same concentration has a higher pH because its [H+] is far lower than the acid concentration

callouts.p: A higher pH does not prove an acid is weak - it could be a strong acid that is more dilute. You must compare at equal concentrations.

core.h: Distinguishing a strong and a weak acid in the lab
core.p: To show that two acids differ in strength, you must use solutions of **the same concentration** and the same volume and temperature, then compare a property that depends on H+ concentration.
bullets: Measure the pH with a pH meter (or universal indicator): the weak acid has the higher pH
Add identical pieces of magnesium ribbon: the strong acid fizzes faster and the Mg dissolves sooner
Add equal masses of calcium carbonate chips: the strong acid gives faster fizzing of CO2
Measure electrical conductivity: the strong acid conducts better because it has more ions
Keep control variables the same: concentration, volume, temperature, mass/surface area of solid

callouts.p: In 'how could you show' questions, always say the acids must be at the **same concentration** - this is usually a marking point.

core.h: Strength is not the same as hazard
core.p: Students often think weak acids are 'safe' and strong acids are 'dangerous'. The hazard depends heavily on concentration too.
bullets: Concentrated ethanoic acid (a weak acid) is corrosive and can burn skin
Very dilute hydrochloric acid (a strong acid) is only an irritant or low hazard
Weak acids such as citric and ethanoic acids are used in foods only because they are used as dilute solutions
So describe hazards using both words, e.g. 'dilute strong acid'

analogy.t: A crowd of people holding balloons
analogy.p: Imagine each acid molecule is a person holding a balloon (the H+ ion). **Concentration** is how many people are packed into the room. **Strength** is how many of them let go of their balloons: in a strong acid everyone lets go, so the ceiling fills with balloons (lots of free H+); in a weak acid only about one person in a hundred lets go at any moment, and some people grab balloons back (reversible). A packed room of 'weak' people can still release as many balloons as a nearly empty room of 'strong' people. Where it breaks down: in a real weak acid, molecules are constantly dissociating and re-forming at the same rate, and when free H+ ions are used up in a reaction, more molecules release theirs - so in the end all the 'balloons' can be used, which the picture does not show well.

terms.d: The substance that dissolves in a solvent to form a solution (here, the acid).
The liquid in which a solute dissolves (here, water).
The amount of solute in a given volume of solution, measured in g/dm3 or mol/dm3.
A solution with a large amount of solute in a given volume.
A solution with a small amount of solute in a given volume.
Adding solvent (water) to a solution so that the same amount of solute is in a larger volume, lowering concentration.
The splitting of a molecule into ions when it dissolves in water, e.g. HCl → H+ + Cl-.
The proportion of acid molecules that have split into ions in solution.
An acid that is completely dissociated into ions in aqueous solution.
An acid that is only partially dissociated into ions in aqueous solution.
A reaction that can go in both directions, shown by ⇌, as in the dissociation of a weak acid.
HCl(aq), a strong acid; fully dissociated into H+ and Cl- ions.
CH3COOH, a weak acid found in vinegar; partially dissociated into CH3COO- and H+ ions.
A weak acid found in citrus fruits.
H2CO3, a weak acid formed when carbon dioxide dissolves in water.
Unit of concentration: moles of solute per cubic decimetre (1000 cm3) of solution.

mistakes.w: A strong acid is a concentrated acid.
mistakes.r: A strong acid is fully dissociated into ions; concentration is a separate idea (amount of acid per volume).

mistakes.w: A weak acid is a dilute acid / has lots of water in it.
mistakes.r: A weak acid is only partially dissociated into ions; it can be concentrated or dilute.

mistakes.w: Strong acids dissolve completely in water.
mistakes.r: Strong acids dissociate (ionise) completely into ions - dissolving is not the same as dissociating.

mistakes.w: Dilute means the acid is weak.
mistakes.r: Dilute means a small amount of acid (solute) in a given volume of solution.

mistakes.w: Adding water makes a strong acid weak.
mistakes.r: Adding water makes it more dilute; it is still a strong acid (still fully dissociated).

mistakes.w: Ethanoic acid has a higher pH so it is weaker (with no mention of concentration).
mistakes.r: Comparing pH only shows strength if both acids have the same concentration.

mistakes.w: The strong acid makes more hydrogen gas with magnesium.
mistakes.r: It makes the gas faster; the same amount of each acid gives the same total volume of hydrogen.

mistakes.w: CH3COOH → CH3COO- + H+
mistakes.r: CH3COOH ⇌ CH3COO- + H+ (reversible arrow for a weak acid).

mistakes.w: Strong acids react faster because they are stronger.
mistakes.r: They have a higher concentration of H+ ions, so more frequent collisions with the reactant particles.

exam.q: State what is meant by a dilute solution of an acid.
model: A small amount of acid (solute) dissolved in a given volume of solution / water
exam.tip: Use 'amount' and 'volume' in your answer.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by a strong acid.
model: An acid that is fully / completely dissociated (ionised) into ions in aqueous solution
exam.tip: 'Dissociated' or 'ionised' is the key word - not 'dissolved'.

exam.q: Give one example of a strong acid and one example of a weak acid.
model: Strong: hydrochloric / nitric / sulfuric acid
Weak: ethanoic / citric / carbonic acid
exam.tip: Spell names correctly: ethanoic, not ethonic.

exam.q: Write an equation to show the dissociation of ethanoic acid in water.
model: CH3COOH → CH3COO- + H+ (correct species)
Reversible arrow ⇌ used
exam.tip: The reversible arrow is usually its own mark.

exam.q: Explain the difference between a concentrated acid and a strong acid.
model: Concentrated: a large amount of acid in a given volume of solution
Strong: fully dissociated into ions (whatever the concentration)
exam.tip: Define both terms separately; do not just say 'they are different'.

exam.q: A student says 'vinegar is a weak acid because it is mostly water'. Explain why the student is wrong.
model: Being mostly water means the solution is dilute
Ethanoic acid is weak because it is only partially dissociated into ions
exam.tip: Spot the confusion between dilute and weak and correct both parts.

exam.q: Hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid of the same concentration are tested with a pH meter. Predict and explain which has the lower pH.
model: Hydrochloric acid has the lower pH
Hydrochloric acid is fully dissociated; ethanoic acid only partially dissociated
So hydrochloric acid has a higher concentration of hydrogen ions
exam.tip: Three marks: prediction, dissociation, H+ concentration.

exam.q: Explain why magnesium reacts faster with 1 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid than with 1 mol/dm3 ethanoic acid.
model: Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid / fully dissociated
so it has a higher concentration of H+ ions
so more frequent collisions between H+ ions and magnesium
exam.tip: Link strength to H+ concentration, then to collision frequency.

exam.q: (Higher) A strong acid has pH 2. It is diluted with water so its hydrogen ion concentration decreases by a factor of 10. State its new pH and whether it is still a strong acid.
model: pH 3
Yes, still strong - it is still fully dissociated; it is just more dilute
exam.tip: Dilution changes concentration, never strength.

exam.q: Excess magnesium is added to 50 cm3 of 1 mol/dm3 HCl and to 50 cm3 of 1 mol/dm3 ethanoic acid. Explain why both produce the same total volume of hydrogen.
model: Both contain the same amount (moles) of acid / same number of acid molecules
As H+ ions react, more ethanoic acid molecules dissociate until all have reacted
exam.tip: Strength changes rate, not the final amount when acid is limiting.

exam.q: Describe how you could show that ethanoic acid is a weaker acid than hydrochloric acid. Explain the expected results in terms of ions.
model: Use solutions of the same concentration, same volume and same temperature
Measure pH with a pH meter / universal indicator
Ethanoic acid will have a higher pH
Add identical pieces of magnesium (or equal masses of calcium carbonate) and compare rate of bubbling
Hydrochloric acid will fizz faster
Hydrochloric acid fully dissociated; ethanoic acid only partially dissociated
So HCl has higher H+ concentration: lower pH and more frequent collisions
exam.tip: Plan (fair test) + results + ion explanation = full marks.

worked.q: 25 g of citric acid is dissolved in water to make 500 cm3 of solution. Calculate the concentration in g/dm3. Is the solution strong or weak?
steps: Convert volume: 500 cm3 / 1000 = 0.5 dm3
Concentration = mass / volume = 25 / 0.5
Citric acid is a weak acid whatever its concentration (partially dissociated)
worked.ans: 50 g/dm3; it is a weak acid - the concentration tells you how much acid is present, not its strength.

worked.q: (Higher) Hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.1 mol/dm3 has pH 1. A student dilutes 10 cm3 of it to 1000 cm3 with water. Calculate the new concentration and predict the pH.
steps: Volume increases by a factor of 1000 / 10 = 100
New concentration = 0.1 / 100 = 0.001 mol/dm3
[H+] has fallen by a factor of 100 = 10 x 10
pH increases by 2: 1 + 2 = 3
worked.ans: 0.001 mol/dm3, pH 3. It is now a dilute strong acid - still fully dissociated.

worked.q: Model answer: Solution X is 2 mol/dm3 ethanoic acid and solution Y is 0.001 mol/dm3 hydrochloric acid. Describe each using the terms strong/weak and concentrated/dilute, and explain why they might have similar pH values.
steps: X: concentrated (large amount of acid per dm3) and weak (partially dissociated)
Y: dilute (small amount of acid per dm3) and strong (fully dissociated)
pH depends on the concentration of H+ ions
X has lots of acid but only a small fraction dissociates; Y has little acid but all of it dissociates
Both effects can give a similar overall H+ concentration
worked.ans: X is a concentrated weak acid; Y is a dilute strong acid. Their H+ concentrations, and so pH values (both about 3), can be similar because pH depends on both concentration and degree of dissociation.

chem_edx.3.3.summary: A **base** is any substance that reacts with an acid to form a **salt and water only**, and an **alkali** is a base that dissolves in water (a soluble base). Acids react in predictable ways: with **metals** to give a salt and hydrogen, with **metal oxides and metal hydroxides** to give a salt and water, and with **metal carbonates** to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide. You must be able to predict the salt, write balanced equations, and describe the chemical tests for the two gases: hydrogen gives a **squeaky pop** with a lighted splint and carbon dioxide turns **limewater milky (cloudy)**.

core.p: In chemistry a **base** is defined by what it does, not what it looks like. A base is any substance that **reacts with an acid to form a salt and water only**. Most bases are **metal oxides** and **metal hydroxides**. When a base reacts with an acid, the acid's hydrogen ions are used up, so the acidity is removed: this is **neutralisation**.
bullets: Examples of bases: copper(II) oxide CuO, magnesium oxide MgO, zinc oxide ZnO, calcium hydroxide Ca(OH)2, sodium hydroxide NaOH.
Many bases are **insoluble** in water (e.g. copper(II) oxide, zinc oxide, iron(III) oxide).
The word **only** matters: metal carbonates also neutralise acids but they give carbon dioxide as well, so strictly they are not bases by this definition.
A base reacts with the **H+ ions** from the acid, removing them, so the pH rises towards 7.

callouts.p: A base is any substance that reacts with an acid to form a salt and water only.

core.p: An **alkali** is a base that **dissolves in water**. When it dissolves it releases **hydroxide ions, OH-(aq)**, which make the solution alkaline (pH above 7). So every alkali is a base, but not every base is an alkali.
bullets: Common alkalis: sodium hydroxide NaOH, potassium hydroxide KOH, calcium hydroxide Ca(OH)2 (slightly soluble, its solution is limewater) and ammonia solution.
Copper(II) oxide is a base but NOT an alkali because it is insoluble in water.
Alkali solutions contain OH- ions; acid solutions contain H+ ions.
Think of bases as the big family and alkalis as the soluble members of that family.

callouts.p: An alkali is a soluble base. It dissolves in water to produce hydroxide ions, OH-.

callouts.t: Base is not the same as alkali
callouts.p: Do not write that all bases are alkalis. Only bases that dissolve in water are alkalis.

core.h: Salts and how to name them
core.p: A **salt** is the compound formed when the hydrogen in an acid is replaced by a metal (or by ammonium). The **first part** of the name comes from the metal in the base, metal or carbonate. The **second part** comes from the acid.
bullets: **Hydrochloric acid** HCl makes **chlorides** (Cl-).
**Sulfuric acid** H2SO4 makes **sulfates** (SO4 2-).
**Nitric acid** HNO3 makes **nitrates** (NO3-).
Example: zinc + sulfuric acid gives zinc sulfate; copper(II) oxide + nitric acid gives copper(II) nitrate.
Keep roman numerals for transition metals, e.g. iron(II) chloride, copper(II) sulfate.
To work out a formula, balance the charges: Mg2+ with Cl- gives MgCl2; Na+ with SO4 2- gives Na2SO4.

callouts.p: Metal name first, acid part second: 'magnesium chloride', never 'chloride magnesium' or 'magnesium chlorine'.

fig.cap: The four general reactions of acids. Every one makes a salt; only the other products change. Metals give hydrogen, oxides and hydroxides give water, carbonates give water and carbon dioxide.
