core.h: Step 1: measure the alkali with a pipette
core.p: Rinse the pipette with a little of the alkali, then use a **pipette filler** to draw up alkali until the **bottom of the meniscus** is on the line. Run it into a clean conical flask.
bullets: Rinse the pipette with **the alkali**, not water: water would dilute the alkali
Never pipette by mouth: use a **pipette filler**
Read the line at **eye level**, using the bottom of the meniscus
Let the pipette drain; touch the tip on the inside of the flask but do not blow out the last drop
The conical flask may be rinsed with **distilled water**: extra water does not change the number of moles of alkali

callouts.p: Burette rinsed with acid, pipette rinsed with alkali, flask rinsed with distilled water. Examiners love asking which liquid each is rinsed with and why.

core.p: Add **a few drops** of a suitable indicator to the alkali. A suitable indicator gives a **single, sharp colour change** at the end point. **Phenolphthalein** or **methyl orange** are used. Universal indicator is **not suitable** because it changes colour gradually through many colours, so the exact end point cannot be seen.
bullets: **Phenolphthalein**: **pink** in alkali → **colourless** in acid
**Methyl orange**: **yellow** in alkali → **red** in acid (orange at the end point)
Only a few drops: indicators are weak acids themselves and too much affects the result
Universal indicator / litmus: gradual or unclear change, so not used for titrations

callouts.p: The point in a titration at which the indicator changes colour, showing that the acid has exactly neutralised the alkali.

core.h: Step 3: fill and read the burette
core.p: Rinse the burette with a little of the acid, then fill it using a small funnel. Run some acid through the tap so the **tip is full** (no air bubble), **remove the funnel**, and record the **initial reading**.
bullets: Rinse with **the acid** so the acid is not diluted by water left inside
Fill the jet below the tap: an air bubble would make the measured volume wrong
Remove the funnel: drips from it would add acid you have not measured
Read at **eye level**, from the **bottom of the meniscus**
Record readings to **2 decimal places**, ending in 0 or 5 (e.g. 0.00, 23.85 cm3)
Burette scale reads **downwards**: 0 at the top

fig.cap: Reading a burette: keep your eye level with the liquid and read the bottom of the meniscus. Burette numbers increase downwards, so this reading is 21.70 cm3.

core.h: Step 4: titrate to the end point
core.p: Place the flask on a **white tile** under the burette. Open the tap and add acid while **swirling** the flask. As the colour starts to change where the acid lands, slow down and add the acid **drop by drop** until the indicator **just changes colour** permanently. Record the final reading.
bullets: Swirling **mixes** the acid and alkali so the whole solution reacts and the colour change is not local
Near the end point add **dropwise** so you do not overshoot
Wash the inside of the flask with a little distilled water to rinse down drops on the walls
**Titre** = final reading − initial reading
First run is a **rough** (trial) titration to find the approximate end point
Repeat **accurately** until you have **concordant** titres (within 0.10 cm3 of each other), then calculate a mean of the concordant titres

callouts.p: The volume of solution added from the burette to reach the end point.
If you add acid too quickly you go past the end point. Then the flask contains excess acid and that run must be discarded.

core.p: The indicator is an impurity in the salt solution. So once you know the exact volume of acid needed, **repeat the titration with a fresh 25.0 cm3 of alkali but no indicator**, adding exactly the mean titre of acid. This gives a solution of **pure salt and water**.
bullets: Mix the **same volumes** of acid and alkali as found in the titration
**No indicator** this time, so the salt is not contaminated with indicator
The resulting solution should be neutral (pH 7 for a strong acid with a strong alkali)
This solution now contains only the dissolved salt and water

callouts.p: The titration is repeated without the indicator so that the salt is not contaminated by the indicator.

core.h: Step 6: crystallise and dry the salt
core.p: Pour the neutral salt solution into an **evaporating basin** and heat it to **evaporate some of the water** until the **crystallisation point**. Leave it to **cool** so crystals form, then filter them off and dry them.
bullets: Heat gently (e.g. on a water bath) to avoid spitting
Test for the crystallisation point with a glass rod: crystals form on it as it cools
Leave to cool slowly: the salt is less soluble when cold, so crystals form
**Filter** to collect the crystals
**Dry** by patting between filter papers or leaving in a warm place / drying oven
Evaporating fully to dryness can make the solid spit and, for hydrated salts, removes water of crystallisation

callouts.p: Pure comes from the exact volumes and no indicator. Dry comes from patting with filter paper or a warm oven. Mention both in a 6-mark answer.

core.h: What happens to pH during the titration
core.p: As acid is added to alkali in the flask, the pH falls slowly at first because there is still lots of OH- left. Close to the end point, a single drop removes the last OH- ions and the pH **drops very steeply**. This sudden change is why an indicator with one sharp colour change works well.
bullets: Start: excess OH-, high pH (around 13 for dilute sodium hydroxide)
End point: H+ and OH- have exactly reacted; pH 7 for strong acid + strong alkali
After: excess H+, low pH (around 1)
A sharp indicator changes colour within this steep vertical section

fig.cap: pH in the flask as acid is added to alkali. The pH falls steeply near the end point, so one or two drops change the indicator colour sharply.

core.h: Improving accuracy and sources of error
core.p: Grade 9 answers explain how each step affects the result. Most errors give a wrong volume of acid, which means excess acid or alkali contaminates the salt.
bullets: Air bubble in burette jet → titre recorded wrongly
Funnel left in burette → extra acid drips in
Burette rinsed with water instead of acid → acid diluted, titre too large
Not swirling → local colour change, end point misjudged
Reading the top of the meniscus or not at eye level → **parallax error**
Use concordant results only; ignore the rough titration when finding the mean

analogy.t: Filling a glass exactly to the brim
analogy.p: Imagine you need a glass filled exactly to the brim, with no overflow and no gap. You pour quickly at first, then slow to a trickle and finally drip, watching closely. The burette is your jug, the end point is the brim, and the indicator is the moment the surface reaches the top. Once you know exactly how much the glass holds, you can pour that amount next time without watching (no indicator) and still hit the brim. Where it breaks down: in a titration the acid and alkali react to form new substances (salt and water) rather than just filling a space, and the 'brim' is detected by a colour change of a chemical, not by eye on a level.

terms.d: A method of finding the exact volume of one solution that reacts completely with a known volume of another.
A soluble base that forms OH- ions in aqueous solution.
The reaction between an acid and a base to form a salt and water; H+ + OH- → H2O.
A long graduated tube with a tap that delivers accurately measured, variable volumes of liquid, read to 0.05 cm3.
Glassware that measures and delivers one fixed, accurate volume of liquid, e.g. 25.0 cm3.
A safety bulb used to draw liquid into a pipette instead of using the mouth.
A substance that changes colour depending on whether a solution is acidic or alkaline.
An indicator that is pink in alkali and colourless in acid.
An indicator that is yellow in alkali and red in acid.
The point at which the indicator changes colour, showing the reactants have exactly neutralised each other.
The volume of solution added from the burette to reach the end point (final minus initial reading).
Titres that agree closely, usually within 0.10 cm3 of each other.
The curved surface of a liquid in a tube; read from the bottom of the curve at eye level.
The point at which a hot solution is saturated so crystals form on cooling.
A compound formed when the hydrogen in an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion.
An error in reading a scale caused by not having the eye level with the mark.

mistakes.w: Use universal indicator so you can see the pH.
mistakes.r: Use **phenolphthalein or methyl orange**, which give a **sharp single colour change**; universal indicator changes gradually.

mistakes.w: Add an excess of sodium hydroxide and filter off what is left.
mistakes.r: Sodium hydroxide is **soluble**, so excess cannot be filtered off; a **titration** finds the exact volumes.

mistakes.w: Rinse the burette with distilled water before filling.
mistakes.r: Rinse the burette with **the acid** it will contain, so the acid is not diluted.

mistakes.w: The white tile is to protect the bench.
mistakes.r: The white tile makes the **colour change easier to see**.

mistakes.w: Evaporate the solution containing the indicator to get the salt.
mistakes.r: **Repeat without indicator** using the same volumes, so the salt is not contaminated.

mistakes.w: Phenolphthalein turns from colourless to pink when acid is added to alkali.
mistakes.r: Adding acid to alkali: phenolphthalein goes **pink → colourless**.

mistakes.w: Read the burette from the top of the meniscus to 1 decimal place.
mistakes.r: Read the **bottom of the meniscus at eye level**, to **2 decimal places** (nearest 0.05 cm3).

mistakes.w: Include the rough titration in the mean.
mistakes.r: Use only **concordant** titres (within 0.10 cm3) to calculate the mean.

mistakes.w: Boil the salt solution until dry.
mistakes.r: Heat to the **crystallisation point**, leave to **cool and crystallise**, filter, then dry.

exam.q: Name the piece of apparatus used to measure exactly 25.0 cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution.
model: Pipette (with pipette filler)
exam.tip: A measuring cylinder is not accurate enough and does not score.

exam.q: Name a suitable indicator for this titration and give its colour change when hydrochloric acid is added to sodium hydroxide.
model: Phenolphthalein
Pink to colourless
exam.tip: Or methyl orange: yellow to red/orange. The direction of change matters.

exam.q: Explain why universal indicator is not used in a titration.
model: It has a gradual colour change / many colours
So the exact end point is hard to see
exam.tip: The word 'sharp' is what examiners want for a suitable indicator.

exam.q: Give the reason for placing the conical flask on a white tile.
model: To see the colour change (end point) more clearly
exam.tip: One-mark questions want the one precise reason.

exam.q: Explain why the flask is swirled while acid is added from the burette.
model: To mix the acid and alkali
So that the colour change shows when all the alkali has reacted / not just locally
exam.tip: Link mixing to accuracy of the end point.

exam.q: Explain why the titration is repeated without indicator before the salt is crystallised.
model: The same volumes of acid and alkali are mixed
So the salt is not contaminated with indicator / is pure
exam.tip: The idea of the indicator being an impurity is the key mark.

exam.q: Explain why sodium chloride is made by titration but copper sulfate can be made by adding excess copper oxide to acid.
model: Sodium hydroxide is soluble / an alkali
Excess sodium hydroxide could not be removed by filtering
Copper oxide is insoluble so its excess can be filtered off
exam.tip: Compare solubility of the base in both methods.

exam.q: Write the ionic equation for the reaction between any acid and any alkali.
model: H+(aq) + OH-(aq) → H2O(l)
exam.tip: State symbols are often required on Higher papers.

exam.q: A student's titres were 24.60 (rough), 23.80, 24.30 and 23.90 cm3. Identify the concordant titres and calculate the mean titre.
model: Concordant: 23.80 and 23.90 cm3
Mean = 23.85 cm3
exam.tip: Leave out the rough and any result more than 0.10 cm3 away.

exam.q: Give two reasons why the burette should be rinsed with the acid and the funnel removed before titrating.
model: Rinsing with acid stops it being diluted by water left in the burette
Removing the funnel stops drips of extra acid changing the reading
exam.tip: Each reason should say what would go wrong.

exam.q: Describe how to use a titration to prepare a pure, dry sample of sodium chloride from dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution.
model: Use a pipette (and filler) to put 25.0 cm3 sodium hydroxide into a conical flask; add a few drops of phenolphthalein/methyl orange
Fill a burette with hydrochloric acid and record the initial reading
Add acid while swirling, dropwise near the end point, until the indicator just changes colour; record the volume used
Repeat to get concordant results / find mean titre
Repeat with the same volumes of acid and alkali but without indicator
Evaporate some water until crystallisation point, leave to cool and crystallise, filter and dry the crystals (pat with filter paper / warm oven)
exam.tip: Order matters. Make sure 'without indicator' and 'crystallisation' both appear: they are the two steps most often forgotten.

worked.q: A student titrated 25.0 cm3 of sodium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid. Burette readings (cm3): rough 0.00 → 24.55; run 1 0.20 → 24.10; run 2 0.05 → 24.00; run 3 1.00 → 24.90. Find the mean titre and the volume of acid to use when repeating without indicator.
steps: Titre = final − initial
Rough = 24.55 cm3 (ignore for the mean)
All three accurate runs are within 0.10 cm3, so they are concordant
worked.ans: Mean titre is 23.92 cm3 (about 23.90 cm3); add this volume of acid to a fresh 25.0 cm3 of alkali with no indicator.

worked.q: (Chemistry only, Higher) 25.0 cm3 of 0.100 mol/dm3 sodium hydroxide is exactly neutralised by hydrochloric acid. Calculate the maximum mass of sodium chloride that can be crystallised. (Mr NaCl = 58.5)
steps: Moles NaOH = concentration × volume in dm3 = 0.100 × (25.0 ÷ 1000) = 0.00250 mol
NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O, so the mole ratio NaOH : NaCl = 1 : 1
Moles NaCl = 0.00250 mol
worked.ans: Maximum mass of sodium chloride = 0.146 g.

worked.q: Potassium sulfate is made by titrating potassium hydroxide solution with dilute sulfuric acid. Write the balanced equation and explain why this salt is prepared by titration.
steps: Word: potassium hydroxide + sulfuric acid → potassium sulfate + water
Formulae: KOH, H2SO4, K2SO4, H2O
Balance K: 2KOH; balance H and O: 2H2O
2KOH(aq) + H2SO4(aq) → K2SO4(aq) + 2H2O(l)
Potassium hydroxide is soluble, so any excess could not be filtered off; the exact volumes must be found by titration
worked.ans: 2KOH + H2SO4 → K2SO4 + 2H2O; a titration is used because both reactants are soluble.

chem_edx.3.8.summary: A small set of **solubility rules** lets you predict whether a salt dissolves in water: **all sodium, potassium and ammonium salts and all nitrates are soluble**, most chlorides and sulfates are soluble (with named exceptions), and most carbonates and hydroxides are **insoluble**. When two solutions are mixed and their ions can combine into an insoluble salt, that salt forms as a solid **precipitate**. An insoluble salt is prepared by mixing two suitable soluble salt solutions, then **filtering**, **washing with distilled water** and **drying** the precipitate.

core.h: Soluble and insoluble: what it means
core.p: A substance is **soluble** if it dissolves in water to form a solution, and **insoluble** if it does not dissolve (or only very slightly). For ionic salts, dissolving means the ions separate and spread through the water. If the attraction between the ions in the lattice is too strong compared with their attraction to water molecules, the salt stays as a solid: it is insoluble.
bullets: Soluble salt in water → ions free to move, e.g. NaCl(aq) is Na+(aq) and Cl-(aq)
Insoluble salt → stays as a solid, shown with state symbol **(s)**
The rules below are for **common** salts at GCSE; you learn them, you do not derive them
Knowing solubility tells you **which method** to use to make a salt: soluble salts by crystallisation, insoluble salts by **precipitation**

callouts.p: An insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed together.

core.p: These are the exact rules the spec lists. Learn them word for word: questions often give two solutions and ask whether a precipitate forms.
bullets: **Rule 1**: all common **sodium, potassium and ammonium** salts are **soluble**
**Rule 2**: all **nitrates** are **soluble**
**Rule 3**: common **chlorides** are soluble **except silver chloride and lead chloride**
**Rule 4**: common **sulfates** are soluble **except lead sulfate, barium sulfate and calcium sulfate**
**Rule 5**: common **carbonates and hydroxides** are **insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and ammonium**

callouts.p: 'SNAP' salts always dissolve: Sodium, Nitrate, Ammonium, Potassium. Chloride exceptions: 'Silver and Lead'. Sulfate exceptions: 'Lead, Barium, Calcium'.

core.h: Using the rules on a single compound
core.p: To decide whether one compound is soluble, check the rules **in order**. Rules 1 and 2 override everything else, so check the metal (or ammonium) and the nitrate first.
bullets: Is it a sodium, potassium or ammonium compound? → **soluble** (e.g. sodium carbonate)
Is it a nitrate? → **soluble** (e.g. silver nitrate, lead nitrate)
Is it a chloride? → soluble unless silver or lead
Is it a sulfate? → soluble unless lead, barium or calcium
Is it a carbonate or hydroxide? → **insoluble** unless sodium, potassium or ammonium
Examples: copper carbonate insoluble; barium chloride soluble; lead nitrate soluble; magnesium hydroxide insoluble
Note: calcium hydroxide is only **slightly** soluble, which is why limewater is a dilute solution

callouts.p: Lead nitrate and silver nitrate are both soluble (all nitrates are). That is exactly why they are used as starting solutions to make insoluble lead and silver salts.

core.h: What happens when solutions are mixed
core.p: Two salt solutions contain four kinds of ion moving freely. When you mix them, the ions can **swap partners**. If any combination of a positive ion from one solution and a negative ion from the other is **insoluble**, those ions lock together into a solid lattice and appear as a cloudy **precipitate**. The other ions stay dissolved.
bullets: Write down the two new possible combinations (swap partners)
Use the rules to decide whether each new compound is soluble
If one is insoluble → a **precipitate** of that compound forms
If both are soluble → **no precipitate**; the ions just stay mixed in solution
Precipitation reactions are usually **very fast** because ions in solution meet instantly
The ions that stay in solution and do not change are called **spectator ions**

callouts.p: AB(aq) + CD(aq) → AD + CB. Check AD and CB with the solubility rules. The insoluble one gets (s) and is the precipitate.

core.p: An ionic equation shows only the ions that **actually react**, leaving out spectator ions. For a precipitation reaction, it shows the two ions joining to form the solid.
bullets: Barium sulfate: **Ba2+(aq) + SO4 2-(aq) → BaSO4(s)**
Silver chloride: **Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) → AgCl(s)**
Lead chloride: Pb2+(aq) + 2Cl-(aq) → PbCl2(s)
Calcium carbonate: Ca2+(aq) + CO3 2-(aq) → CaCO3(s)
Copper(II) hydroxide: Cu2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) → Cu(OH)2(s)
Charges must balance on both sides as well as atoms
The same ionic equation applies whichever soluble salts supplied the ions: Ba2+ from barium chloride or barium nitrate gives the same reaction with sulfate

callouts.p: Ions that are present in the reaction mixture but do not take part in the reaction; they are left out of the ionic equation.

core.p: Exam questions name two solutions and ask you to predict whether a precipitate forms and to **name it**. Always show the swap and give the name of the insoluble product, not just 'yes'.
bullets: Silver nitrate + sodium chloride → silver chloride (**insoluble, white precipitate**) + sodium nitrate (soluble)
Barium chloride + sodium sulfate → barium sulfate (**white precipitate**) + sodium chloride
Lead nitrate + sodium chloride → lead chloride (**white precipitate**) + sodium nitrate
Calcium chloride + sodium carbonate → calcium carbonate (**white precipitate**) + sodium chloride
Copper sulfate + sodium hydroxide → copper hydroxide (**blue precipitate**) + sodium sulfate
Potassium chloride + sodium nitrate → potassium nitrate + sodium chloride: **both soluble, no precipitate**
Ammonium sulfate + sodium chloride → **no precipitate**

core.h: Choosing reactants to make an insoluble salt
core.p: To make insoluble salt XY, you need one solution that supplies the **positive ion X** and another that supplies the **negative ion Y**. Both starting compounds must be **soluble**, and the other product must also be **soluble** so it can be washed away. The easiest way is to pick a **nitrate** for the metal ion and a **sodium or potassium** salt for the negative ion.
bullets: Metal ion source: usually the **metal nitrate** (all nitrates are soluble), e.g. lead nitrate, silver nitrate, barium nitrate
Barium chloride and calcium chloride are also soluble and commonly used
Negative ion source: a **sodium or potassium** salt, e.g. sodium sulfate, sodium carbonate, sodium chloride
By-product is then a sodium/potassium nitrate or chloride: **soluble**, so it stays in the filtrate
Example: lead sulfate from **lead nitrate + sodium sulfate**
Example: calcium carbonate from **calcium chloride + sodium carbonate**

callouts.t: Why not use the insoluble base?
callouts.p: You cannot make barium sulfate by adding barium carbonate to sulfuric acid and filtering, because the barium sulfate would coat the solid and itself be filtered out with the excess. Insoluble salts are made by precipitation.

core.h: Method: preparing a pure, dry insoluble salt
core.p: This is the method the spec asks you to describe. Each step either makes the precipitate, separates it, removes impurities, or dries it.
bullets: 1. Dissolve each soluble salt in **distilled water** (or use the solutions provided) in separate beakers
2. **Mix** the two solutions in a beaker and **stir**: the precipitate forms immediately
3. **Filter** the mixture using a funnel and filter paper: the precipitate is the **residue**
4. **Wash** the residue on the filter paper with **distilled water** several times
5. Scrape the solid onto fresh filter paper and **dry** it in a **warm oven** (or leave to dry in a warm place / pat dry with filter paper)
Distilled water is used so no new ions are added as impurities
Washing removes the **soluble salt solution** (e.g. sodium nitrate) clinging to the solid

callouts.p: Mix → filter → wash (distilled water) → dry (warm oven). Missing 'wash' is the most common lost mark.

fig.cap: Filtering and washing an insoluble salt. The precipitate stays on the filter paper as the residue; distilled water from a wash bottle rinses away the soluble by-product, which passes into the filtrate.

core.p: Examiners ask for reasons, not just steps. Link every step to the purity or dryness of the final product.
bullets: **Distilled water** for dissolving: tap water contains ions (e.g. Ca2+, Cl-) that could form extra precipitates
**Stirring/mixing**: makes sure all the ions meet so the reaction is complete
**Filtering**: separates the insoluble salt from the solution
**Washing with distilled water**: removes soluble impurities (the other product and any unreacted ions) left on the solid
**Drying in a warm oven**: removes water; a warm (not very hot) oven avoids decomposing the salt
Using roughly equal amounts of each solution avoids wasting reagent; any excess stays in solution and is washed away

callouts.p: Never evaporate the filtrate to get an insoluble salt. The insoluble salt is the solid on the filter paper; the filtrate only contains the soluble by-product.

core.p: The solubility of the salt you want, and of the reactants, decides the method. This links 3.15-3.18 with 3.19-3.21.
bullets: Insoluble salt wanted → **precipitation**: mix two soluble salt solutions, filter, wash, dry
Soluble salt from insoluble base/carbonate/metal → add excess solid to acid, filter, crystallise
Soluble salt from alkali → titration, repeat without indicator, crystallise
In precipitation the product is the **residue**; in the other two methods the product is in the **filtrate**

core.p: Many precipitates are white, but some transition metal compounds are coloured. Knowing them helps you describe what you would observe.
bullets: Silver chloride, AgCl: **white**
Barium sulfate, BaSO4: **white**
Lead chloride and lead sulfate: **white**
Calcium carbonate, CaCO3: **white**
Copper(II) carbonate: **green**; copper(II) hydroxide: **blue**
Iron(II) hydroxide: **green**; iron(III) hydroxide: **orange-brown**
Observation wording: 'a white precipitate forms' or 'the solution turns cloudy/milky'

analogy.p: Two groups arrive at a dance (two solutions), each made of couples (positive and negative ions) who split up as soon as they enter the hall (dissolve). Everyone moves freely. But some pairs, like Ba2+ and SO4 2-, are so attracted to each other that as soon as they meet they hold on tightly and drop out of the dance to sit together on the floor: that is the precipitate. Other dancers (spectator ions) just keep moving around. Filtering is like clearing the floor of those seated couples. Where it breaks down: real ions do not form pairs but a huge lattice of millions of ions, and whether they 'sit down' depends on the strength of attractions compared with water, not on choice.

terms.d: Able to dissolve in water to form a solution.
Does not dissolve (or dissolves only very slightly) in water.
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed together.
A reaction between two solutions that forms an insoluble solid product.
General rules that predict whether common ionic compounds dissolve in water.
Ions present in a reaction mixture that do not take part in the reaction.
An equation showing only the ions that react and the product they form, leaving out spectator ions.
A salt containing the NO3- ion; all nitrates are soluble.
A salt containing the SO4 2- ion; soluble except lead, barium and calcium sulfate.
A salt containing the Cl- ion; soluble except silver chloride and lead chloride.
A salt containing the CO3 2- ion; insoluble except sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonate.
A compound containing the OH- ion; insoluble except sodium, potassium and ammonium hydroxide.
The solid left on the filter paper after filtration; here, the insoluble salt.
The liquid that passes through the filter paper; here, containing the soluble by-product.
Water that has been purified so it contains no dissolved ions.
Dissolved in water.

mistakes.w: Silver nitrate is insoluble because silver salts are insoluble.
mistakes.r: **All nitrates are soluble**, including silver nitrate and lead nitrate.

mistakes.w: All chlorides are soluble.
mistakes.r: Chlorides are soluble **except silver chloride and lead chloride**.

mistakes.w: Sodium carbonate is insoluble because carbonates are insoluble.
mistakes.r: Carbonates are insoluble **except sodium, potassium and ammonium** carbonates, so sodium carbonate is soluble.

mistakes.w: Barium chloride is insoluble because barium sulfate is insoluble.
mistakes.r: Barium **chloride** is soluble; only barium **sulfate** is in the exceptions list.

mistakes.w: To get the insoluble salt, evaporate the filtrate.
mistakes.r: The insoluble salt is the **residue** on the filter paper; filter, **wash with distilled water** and **dry**.

mistakes.w: Wash the precipitate with tap water.
mistakes.r: Wash with **distilled water**, so no extra ions contaminate the salt.

mistakes.w: A precipitate forms when potassium chloride and sodium nitrate are mixed.
mistakes.r: Both possible products (potassium nitrate, sodium chloride) are soluble, so **no precipitate** forms.

mistakes.w: Ba2+ + SO4 2- → BaSO4 (aq)
mistakes.r: The precipitate is a solid: **BaSO4(s)**.

mistakes.w: Make lead chloride by adding lead to hydrochloric acid and crystallising.
mistakes.r: Lead chloride is insoluble: mix **lead nitrate solution with sodium chloride solution**, then filter, wash and dry.

exam.q: State which of these compounds is insoluble in water: sodium sulfate, barium sulfate, copper sulfate, potassium sulfate.
model: Barium sulfate
exam.tip: Sulfate exceptions: lead, barium, calcium.

exam.q: Name the two common chlorides that are insoluble in water.
model: Silver chloride
Lead chloride
exam.tip: Give full names, not just 'silver and lead'.

exam.q: Use the solubility rules to classify sodium carbonate and calcium carbonate as soluble or insoluble, giving the rule for each.
model: Sodium carbonate is soluble (all sodium salts soluble)
Calcium carbonate is insoluble (carbonates insoluble except Na, K, NH4)
exam.tip: Quote the rule that decides each case.

exam.q: Predict whether a precipitate forms when solutions of silver nitrate and sodium chloride are mixed. Name the precipitate if one forms.
model: Yes, a precipitate forms
Silver chloride (white)
exam.tip: Always name the precipitate; 'yes' alone gets one mark at most.

exam.q: Explain why no precipitate forms when potassium nitrate solution is mixed with ammonium chloride solution.
model: Possible products are potassium chloride and ammonium nitrate
Both are soluble (potassium and ammonium salts / nitrates are soluble)
exam.tip: Name both possible products and state why each is soluble.

exam.q: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the formation of barium sulfate.
model: Ba2+ + SO4 2- → BaSO4
exam.tip: The precipitate must be (s).

exam.q: Suggest two solutions that could be mixed to make lead sulfate.
model: Lead nitrate (solution)
Sodium sulfate / potassium sulfate / any soluble sulfate except Ba or Ca (solution)
exam.tip: The lead must come from a soluble lead compound: lead nitrate.

exam.q: Explain why the precipitate is washed with distilled water after filtering.
model: To remove soluble impurities / the other (soluble) product
Distilled water contains no ions so does not add impurities
exam.tip: Two ideas: what is removed, and why distilled.

exam.q: Write the balanced equation, with state symbols, for the reaction between calcium chloride solution and sodium carbonate solution.
model: CaCl2 + Na2CO3 → CaCO3 + 2NaCl
Balanced with 2NaCl
exam.tip: Only the insoluble product gets (s).

exam.q: Describe how you would prepare a pure, dry sample of insoluble barium sulfate starting from two solutions.
model: Choose soluble barium salt, e.g. barium chloride/nitrate solution, and soluble sulfate, e.g. sodium sulfate solution
Mix the two solutions in a beaker and stir
A white precipitate of barium sulfate forms
Filter the mixture; barium sulfate is the residue on the filter paper
Wash the residue with distilled water to remove soluble impurities (e.g. sodium chloride)
Dry in a warm oven / leave to dry / pat dry between filter papers
exam.tip: Name the reagents, then use the verbs mix, filter, wash, dry in that order.

exam.q: A student suggests making silver chloride by adding silver metal to dilute hydrochloric acid and crystallising the solution. Explain two reasons why this would not work.
model: Silver is unreactive / does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid
Silver chloride is insoluble so it cannot be crystallised from solution; it must be made by precipitation (e.g. silver nitrate + sodium chloride)
exam.tip: Use both reactivity and solubility ideas.

worked.q: Predict what happens when copper(II) sulfate solution is mixed with sodium hydroxide solution. Name any precipitate and write the ionic equation.
steps: Ions present: Cu2+, SO4 2-, Na+, OH-
Swap partners: copper(II) hydroxide and sodium sulfate
Copper(II) hydroxide: hydroxides insoluble except Na, K, NH4 → insoluble
Sodium sulfate: all sodium salts soluble → stays dissolved
Precipitate = copper(II) hydroxide, blue
Ionic equation: Cu2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) → Cu(OH)2(s); Na+ and SO4 2- are spectator ions
worked.ans: A blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide forms: Cu2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) → Cu(OH)2(s).

worked.q: Which of these pairs of solutions gives a precipitate? (a) barium nitrate + potassium sulfate (b) sodium chloride + potassium nitrate (c) lead nitrate + sodium chloride
steps: (a) Possible products: barium sulfate and potassium nitrate. Barium sulfate is a sulfate exception → insoluble. Precipitate of barium sulfate
(b) Possible products: sodium nitrate and potassium chloride. Both sodium/potassium salts → soluble. No precipitate
(c) Possible products: lead chloride and sodium nitrate. Lead chloride is a chloride exception → insoluble. Precipitate of lead chloride
worked.ans: (a) barium sulfate precipitate; (b) no precipitate; (c) lead chloride precipitate.

worked.q: Plan the preparation of a pure, dry sample of calcium carbonate. Give the balanced equation.
steps: Calcium carbonate is insoluble (carbonates insoluble except Na, K, NH4), so use precipitation
Ca2+ source: calcium chloride or calcium nitrate solution (soluble)
CO3 2- source: sodium carbonate solution (soluble, sodium salt)
Equation: CaCl2(aq) + Na2CO3(aq) → CaCO3(s) + 2NaCl(aq)
Mix the solutions and stir; a white precipitate forms
Filter; wash the residue with distilled water to remove sodium chloride
Dry in a warm oven
worked.ans: Mix calcium chloride and sodium carbonate solutions; filter, wash with distilled water and dry the white calcium carbonate.

chem_edx.3.9.summary: Electrolysis is the process in which **electrical energy from a direct current (d.c.) supply decomposes an electrolyte**. An **electrolyte** is an ionic compound that is **molten or dissolved in water**, so its ions are free to move and carry charge. When the current flows, **positive cations migrate to the negative cathode** and **negative anions migrate to the positive anode**, where they are discharged as new substances. Understanding why ions must be mobile, why the current must be d.c., and which way each ion moves is the foundation for every other electrolysis question.

core.p: An electrolyte is a liquid or solution that conducts electricity because it contains ions that are free to move. In the Edexcel specification, electrolytes are **ionic compounds in the molten state or dissolved in water**.
bullets: Ionic compounds are made of positive ions (cations) and negative ions (anions) held by strong electrostatic forces.
In a **solid** ionic compound the ions are fixed in a giant ionic lattice and can only vibrate, so the solid **does not conduct**.
When **melted**, the lattice breaks down and ions can move past each other.
When **dissolved in water**, the ions separate and move freely through the solution.
Mobile ions carry charge through the liquid, so the liquid conducts and can be electrolysed.
Examples: molten lead bromide, molten sodium chloride, copper sulfate solution, sodium chloride solution (brine), dilute sulfuric acid.

callouts.p: An ionic compound in the molten state or dissolved in water, which conducts electricity because its ions are free to move.

core.h: Why solid ionic compounds cannot be electrolysed
core.p: Conduction needs charged particles that can move. A solid ionic compound contains charged particles, but they are locked in place, so no charge can flow and no electrolysis happens.
bullets: Ions in a lattice are held by **strong electrostatic attraction** between oppositely charged ions in all directions.
Solid sodium chloride has ions but they are **not free to move**, so it is an insulator.
There are **no delocalised electrons** in ionic compounds, unlike metals.
Heating to the melting point (801 degrees C for NaCl) gives the ions enough energy to break free of fixed positions.
Exam phrase: 'ions are free to move and carry the charge' scores the mark; 'electrons are free to move' does not.

callouts.p: In an electrolyte the current is carried by moving ions. Electrons only flow in the metal wires and electrodes.

core.p: Electrolysis uses electrical energy to break down (decompose) an electrolyte into simpler substances, usually elements. Without the electrical energy the compound would not split up on its own.
bullets: The energy comes from a **direct current (d.c.) supply** such as a battery or power pack set to d.c.
The electrolyte is **decomposed**: for example molten lead bromide forms lead and bromine.
The products form **at the electrodes**, not throughout the liquid.
It is a chemical change: new substances are made and energy is transferred electrically.
Electrolysis is used to extract reactive metals (such as aluminium), to make chlorine and hydrogen from brine, and to purify copper.

callouts.p: A process in which electrical energy, from a direct current supply, decomposes electrolytes.

core.h: Why the supply must be direct current
core.p: A direct current flows in one direction only, so one electrode is always positive and the other is always negative. This makes each type of ion keep moving in one direction to one electrode.
bullets: With **d.c.** the cathode stays negative and the anode stays positive throughout.
Cations always drift to the same electrode and anions to the other, so products build up separately.
With **alternating current (a.c.)** the electrode charges swap many times a second, so ions just shuffle back and forth and products would mix or not separate.
Symbol for a d.c. cell or battery: long line (positive) and short line (negative).

callouts.p: Electrolysis needs a direct current supply so that the electrodes have a fixed charge.

core.p: An electrolytic cell is the apparatus used for electrolysis: a d.c. supply, connecting wires, two electrodes and an electrolyte in a container.
bullets: **Electrodes** are conducting rods that dip into the electrolyte and carry current in and out.
The **cathode** is the electrode connected to the **negative** terminal.
The **anode** is the electrode connected to the **positive** terminal.
**Inert electrodes** (graphite/carbon or platinum) conduct but do not react with the electrolyte or products.
Electrons flow through the external wires from the anode, round the circuit, to the cathode.
A bulb or ammeter in the circuit shows that current is flowing.

callouts.p: PANIC: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

core.p: The two kinds of ion are named after the electrode they travel to. Knowing the charge of each ion tells you its direction straight away.
bullets: **Cations** are **positively charged** ions, usually metal ions or H+ (e.g. Na+, Cu2+, Pb2+, Al3+, H+).
**Anions** are **negatively charged** ions, usually non-metal ions or OH- (e.g. Cl-, Br-, O2-, OH-, SO4 2-).
Cations travel to the **cathode**; anions travel to the **anode**.
Opposite charges attract: this electrostatic attraction is the reason for the movement.

callouts.p: Positively charged cations migrate to the negatively charged cathode and negatively charged anions migrate to the positively charged anode.

core.p: When the supply is switched on, the cathode gains a surplus of electrons (negative) and the anode loses electrons (positive). Each ion is attracted to the electrode of opposite charge and drifts towards it through the liquid.
bullets: Step 1: the d.c. supply pumps electrons onto the cathode, making it negative.
Step 2: electrons are pulled away from the anode, making it positive.
Step 3: cations are **attracted** to the cathode because opposite charges attract.
Step 4: anions are **attracted** to the anode.
Step 5: at the electrodes the ions are **discharged** (gain or lose electrons) to form atoms or molecules.
The movement of ions in the electrolyte plus electrons in the wires completes the circuit.

callouts.p: Always name the ion, its charge and the electrode with its charge: 'positive lead ions are attracted to the negative cathode'.

fig.cap: Ion migration in molten lead bromide: Pb2+ cations drift towards the negative cathode while Br- anions drift towards the positive anode.

core.p: When an ion reaches its electrode it is discharged: it gains or loses electrons and becomes a neutral atom or molecule. This is how the electrolyte is decomposed.
bullets: At the **cathode**, cations **gain electrons** and become atoms (e.g. lead metal).
At the **anode**, anions **lose electrons** and form atoms that often pair up into molecules (e.g. Br2 gas).
Electrons released at the anode travel through the wire to the supply and on to the cathode.
Discharge is why the products appear at the electrode surfaces, as bubbles, a coating or a liquid.
Details of which ions are discharged and half equations are covered in 3.25-3.27.

callouts.p: The ions move through the electrolyte; the change into new substances happens only at the electrodes.

core.p: Molten lead(II) bromide, PbBr2, is the classic demonstration of electrolysis of a molten ionic compound.
bullets: Solid PbBr2 does not conduct; the bulb only lights once the solid **melts**.
Ions present: **Pb2+** and **Br-**.
Pb2+ migrates to the cathode and forms **molten lead**, which collects at the bottom.
Br- migrates to the anode and forms **brown bromine vapour**.
Overall: lead bromide -> lead + bromine; PbBr2(l) -> Pb(l) + Br2(g).
Done in a fume cupboard because bromine vapour is toxic.

callouts.p: Bromine vapour is toxic and corrosive, so carry this out in a fume cupboard.

core.p: When an ionic compound dissolves, its ions move freely in the water, so the solution is an electrolyte. Water itself also provides a few H+ and OH- ions.
bullets: Copper(II) sulfate solution contains Cu2+, SO4 2-, plus H+ and OH- from water.
Cu2+ and H+ (cations) both move to the cathode.
SO4 2- and OH- (anions) both move to the anode.
Sodium chloride solution contains Na+, Cl-, H+ and OH-.
Which ion is actually discharged depends on reactivity, covered in 3.25.
Solutions conduct at room temperature, so no melting is needed.

callouts.p: For any aqueous electrolyte, list four ions: the two from the compound plus H+ and OH- from water.

core.h: Showing ion movement: coloured ions practical
core.p: Ion migration can be seen directly using a coloured salt such as copper(II) chromate or potassium manganate(VII) on damp filter paper or in a gel connected to a d.c. supply.
bullets: A crystal of potassium manganate(VII) placed on filter paper soaked in an electrolyte such as sodium chloride solution.
The purple colour comes from the **MnO4- anion**, so the purple spreads towards the **positive** electrode (anode).
With copper(II) chromate: blue Cu2+ moves to the cathode, yellow CrO4 2- moves to the anode.
This proves ions are charged and move to the oppositely charged electrode.
Reversing the supply reverses the direction of movement.

callouts.p: Colour moving towards one electrode is direct evidence that ions are charged particles that migrate.

fig.cap: Coloured ions on damp filter paper: blue copper ions drift to the cathode and yellow chromate ions drift to the anode, so the colours separate.

core.h: Electrons in wires, ions in liquids
core.p: A complete circuit needs charge to flow all the way round. Two different charge carriers do the job in different parts of the circuit.
bullets: In the **metal wires and electrodes**: delocalised **electrons** flow.
In the **electrolyte**: **ions** move (cations one way, anions the other).
At the electrode surfaces, discharge transfers electrons between ions and electrodes, linking the two.
No electrons travel through the electrolyte itself.
If the electrolyte freezes, ions stop moving and the current stops, even though the wires still conduct.

callouts.p: Writing that electrons flow through the solution loses the mark.

core.p: This point links back to Topic 1: properties of ionic compounds come from their structure, and electrolysis is a direct consequence.
bullets: Ionic compounds have **high melting points** because of strong electrostatic forces in the lattice, so lots of energy is needed to melt them for electrolysis.
This is why molten electrolysis (e.g. aluminium oxide) is energy-expensive.
Covalent substances such as sugar or ethanol solutions do **not** conduct because they contain no ions: they are **non-electrolytes**.
Pure water is a very poor conductor because it contains only a tiny concentration of H+ and OH-.

analogy.t: A school disco with two doors
analogy.p: Imagine a hall full of students wearing either red tops (cations, positive) or blue tops (anions, negative). A DJ (the d.c. supply) puts a magnet-like attraction on the left door for red tops and the right door for blue tops. Once everyone can move around (the hall is a liquid, not packed seats), red tops stream to the left door and blue tops to the right, and at each door they change out of their tops (discharge) and leave as new people (elements). If everyone is stuck in their seats (a solid lattice), nobody moves. If the DJ keeps swapping which door is which (a.c.), people just shuffle back and forth. Where it breaks down: real ions are attracted by electrostatic forces, not choosing to move, and at the electrodes they gain or lose electrons rather than swapping clothes.

terms.d: A process in which electrical energy from a direct current supply decomposes an electrolyte.
An ionic compound that is molten or dissolved in water, which conducts because its ions are free to move.
An atom or group of atoms that has gained or lost electrons and so carries an electric charge.
A positively charged ion; it migrates to the cathode during electrolysis.
A negatively charged ion; it migrates to the anode during electrolysis.
A conducting rod or plate that carries current into or out of the electrolyte.
The negative electrode, connected to the negative terminal of the d.c. supply.
The positive electrode, connected to the positive terminal of the d.c. supply.
An electric current that flows in one direction only, so the electrodes keep a fixed charge.
An electrode, such as graphite or platinum, that conducts but does not react during electrolysis.
Melted into the liquid state by heating.
Dissolved in water, shown by the state symbol (aq).
Break down a compound into simpler substances.
When an ion gains or loses electrons at an electrode to become a neutral atom or molecule.
Move through the electrolyte towards an electrode under electrostatic attraction.
A substance that does not conduct when molten or dissolved because it contains no free ions, such as a sugar solution.

mistakes.w: Solid sodium chloride conducts because it contains ions.
mistakes.r: Solid NaCl does not conduct: the ions are fixed in the lattice and not free to move.

mistakes.w: Electrons move through the electrolyte.
mistakes.r: Ions move through the electrolyte; electrons only flow in the wires and electrodes.

mistakes.w: Electrolysis uses alternating current.
mistakes.r: Electrolysis needs a direct current (d.c.) supply.

mistakes.w: Positive ions go to the anode.
mistakes.r: Positive cations migrate to the negative cathode.

mistakes.w: The anode is negative.
mistakes.r: The anode is positive; the cathode is negative.

mistakes.w: Negative ions are attracted because they are like the electrode.
mistakes.r: Anions are attracted to the anode because opposite charges attract.

mistakes.w: An electrolyte is any liquid that conducts, like mercury.
mistakes.r: An electrolyte is an ionic compound molten or dissolved in water; metals conduct by electrons and are not decomposed.

mistakes.w: Electricity splits the compound throughout the liquid.
mistakes.r: The electrolyte is decomposed when ions are discharged at the electrodes.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term electrolyte.
model: An ionic compound
that is molten or dissolved in water (so ions can move)
exam.tip: Both 'ionic' and 'molten or dissolved' are needed for two marks.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by electrolysis.
model: Electrical energy / a direct current is used
to decompose / break down an electrolyte
exam.tip: Use 'decompose' and 'direct current' from the spec wording.

exam.q: Name the negative electrode.
model: Cathode
exam.tip: PANIC: Positive Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

exam.q: Explain why solid lead bromide does not conduct electricity but molten lead bromide does.
model: Lead bromide is ionic / contains ions
in the solid the ions are fixed in a lattice and cannot move
when molten the ions are free to move and carry charge
exam.tip: Say 'ions', never 'electrons'.

exam.q: Explain the movement of ions during the electrolysis of molten lead bromide.
model: Lead ions are positive (Pb2+)
and are attracted to / move to the negative cathode
bromide ions are negative (Br-)
and are attracted to / move to the positive anode
exam.tip: Name each ion, give its charge and the charge of the electrode it moves to.

exam.q: Give the formulae of all the ions present in copper(II) sulfate solution.
model: Cu2+ and SO4 2-
H+ and OH- (from water)
exam.tip: Do not forget the ions from water in any aqueous electrolyte.

exam.q: Explain why electrolysis must use a d.c. supply rather than an a.c. supply.
model: d.c. flows in one direction so each electrode keeps a fixed charge
so cations always move to the cathode and anions to the anode (products separate)
exam.tip: Link the fixed electrode charge to the direction ions move.

exam.q: A crystal of potassium manganate(VII) is placed on wet filter paper between two electrodes connected to a d.c. supply. The purple colour moves towards one electrode. State which electrode and explain why.
model: Towards the anode / positive electrode
the purple colour is due to the manganate(VII) ion, MnO4-
which is negative so is attracted to the positive electrode
exam.tip: Identify which ion causes the colour and its charge.

exam.q: Which of these is an electrolyte? A solid sodium chloride B sugar solution C molten potassium iodide D liquid ethanol
model: C molten potassium iodide
exam.tip: It must be ionic AND molten or aqueous.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of particles, how an electric current passes around a circuit containing molten zinc chloride, graphite electrodes and copper wires.
model: In the copper wires and graphite electrodes, delocalised electrons flow
zinc chloride contains Zn2+ and Cl- ions
when molten the ions are free to move
Zn2+ ions move to the negative cathode
Cl- ions move to the positive anode
at the electrodes ions gain/lose electrons (are discharged), completing the circuit
exam.tip: A 6-mark answer needs both charge carriers: electrons in wires, ions in the melt, linked by discharge.

worked.q: Molten sodium chloride is electrolysed. Identify the ions, state which electrode each moves to and name the products.
steps: Sodium chloride is ionic: Na+ and Cl-.
It is molten, so the ions are free to move.
Na+ is a cation, so it is attracted to the negative cathode.
Cl- is an anion, so it is attracted to the positive anode.
At the cathode sodium forms; at the anode chlorine gas forms.
worked.ans: Na+ to cathode forming sodium; Cl- to anode forming chlorine. NaCl(l) -> Na(l) + Cl2(g) (balanced: 2NaCl -> 2Na + Cl2).

worked.q: A student says 'solid copper chloride can be electrolysed if a high enough voltage is used'. Evaluate this statement.
steps: Copper chloride is ionic, containing Cu2+ and Cl- ions.
In the solid, ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice by strong electrostatic forces.
Ions cannot move to the electrodes however high the voltage.
There are no delocalised electrons in an ionic solid to carry charge.
It must be melted or dissolved in water first so the ions become mobile.
worked.ans: The statement is wrong: the solid cannot be electrolysed because its ions cannot move; it must be molten or in aqueous solution.

worked.q: List all the ions in dilute sulfuric acid and say which electrode each migrates towards.
steps: Sulfuric acid in water gives H+ and SO4 2- ions.
Water also provides a small amount of H+ and OH-.
Cations: H+ only, so H+ migrates to the cathode.
Anions: SO4 2- and OH-, which migrate to the anode.
worked.ans: H+ to the cathode; SO4 2- and OH- to the anode.
